name: Instructor-led classroom training
description: You teach a group in one room, in a planned order. You explain a little, ask questions, then get people practising with your help.
bestFor: Reach for it when a group needs the same foundations, shared terms or a set procedure, and needs to get them right.

variants.name: Expert seminar
variants.description: A subject expert takes a small group through one topic in depth, with plenty of time for questions.

variants.name: Facilitated workshop
variants.description: Most of the time goes on group tasks, and you guide the work instead of presenting.

variants.name: Masterclass
variants.description: An expert works on real examples from the group in front of everyone and comments as they go.

variants.name: Interactive briefing
variants.description: A short update of 20 to 30 minutes with two or three planned questions to the group.

variants.name: Socratic seminar
variants.description: You teach almost entirely by asking questions about a text or case the group has read beforehand.

variants.name: Panel-led class
variants.description: Two or three experts answer questions from you and the group, in place of a single teacher.

mechanics: Explicit instruction; cognitive load theory; schema acquisition
cautions: It slides into you talking and them listening, with too much content. Halve the content and give at least a third of the time to practice.
theory: Explicit instruction; cognitive load theory; schema acquisition
howTo: Write down what people must be able to do by the end. Cut the content to what serves that.
Open with a problem from their work, then ask what they already know about it.
Teach in chunks of 10 to 15 minutes. After each chunk, ask a question that everyone must answer, on paper or in pairs.
Show one worked example, then do one together, then let people try one alone.
Walk the room while they practise and correct what you see.
Close with a recall check from memory, notes shut. Do not close with a recap slide.
time: 60 to 90 minutes a session, with a break at least every 90 minutes
group: 8 to 16 people, with pairs for practice

name: Interactive lecture
description: A talk broken into short pieces. Every few minutes you stop and make everyone answer a question, predict a result or apply the idea.
bestFor: Reach for it when a larger group needs to grasp an idea quickly and you cannot run small-group practice.

variants.name: Prediction pause
variants.description: You stop before a result or demonstration and ask everyone to commit to a guess first.

variants.name: Audience response lecture
variants.description: Everyone answers on a phone poll or with voting cards, so you can see the spread of answers.

variants.name: Case-interruption lecture
variants.description: You tell a real case in stages and stop at each decision point to ask what the group would do.

variants.name: Think-pair-share lecture
variants.description: For each question people think alone, talk it over with a neighbour, then share with the room.

variants.name: Demonstration lecture
variants.description: You show the skill being done and say what you are noticing and deciding as you go.

variants.name: Question-led lecture
variants.description: The talk is built around four or five big questions, and you answer each only after the room has tried.

mechanics: Generative learning; retrieval; attention and cognitive load
cautions: Polls that ask for opinions or easy facts look lively and teach little. Ask questions people have to think about, and act on the answers you get.
theory: Generative learning; retrieval; attention and cognitive load
howTo: Split the talk into pieces of 8 to 10 minutes, with one idea in each.
Write one question per piece that makes people use the idea, not just repeat it.
Ask the question, then give a silent minute to answer alone, on paper or in a poll.
Give two minutes to compare answers with a neighbour.
Take three or four answers from the room, show the right one and explain the most common wrong one.
End by asking everyone to write the main points from memory.
time: 30 to 45 minutes
group: Any size from 12 to several hundred, with pairs for the questions

name: Worked examples
description: You give learners a problem that is already solved, with every step and the reason for it written out. They study it before they try one of their own.
bestFor: Reach for it when people are new to a procedure or a type of problem that has several steps.

variants.name: Annotated worked example
variants.description: Notes in the margin explain why each step is taken.

variants.name: Comparative worked examples
variants.description: Two or three examples sit side by side and learners say what is the same and what differs.

variants.name: Error-containing worked example
variants.description: The example has a planted mistake that learners must find and fix.

variants.name: Video worked example
variants.description: The solution is recorded on video, so learners can pause and replay each step.

variants.name: Partially completed example
variants.description: Some steps are left blank for the learner to fill in.

variants.name: Expert-versus-novice example
variants.description: An expert's solution sits beside a beginner's, and learners say what the expert did differently.

mechanics: Cognitive load theory; worked-example effect
cautions: People skim an example and think they have it, so make them explain each step and then solve a similar problem. Once people can do the task, move them on to problems without examples.
theory: Cognitive load theory; worked-example effect
howTo: Pick a typical problem from the work. Write out the full solution, with a short note at each step saying why.
Give people five minutes to read it alone.
In pairs, ask them to explain each step to each other in their own words.
Give a second example that looks different but uses the same method. Ask what stayed the same.
Follow straight away with a similar problem to solve with the examples out of sight.
time: 15 to 25 minutes for a pair of examples and one problem
group: Alone first, then pairs, any group size

name: Faded worked examples
description: A run of similar problems where you solve a little less each time. Learners start with a full example and finish by solving one alone.
bestFor: Reach for it when people have seen a procedure and now need to get to doing it without help.

variants.name: Completion problem sequence
variants.description: Each problem comes part solved and learners finish it.

variants.name: Progressive prompt removal
variants.description: Learners do every step, and you take away the hints one at a time.

variants.name: Scaffold fading by mastery
variants.description: A learner only moves to less support after getting the current level right, say twice in a row.

variants.name: Peer-supported fading
variants.description: A partner gives the help at first and then steps back, in place of the worksheet.

variants.name: AI-adaptive scaffold fading
variants.description: An AI tutor gives or holds back hints based on each answer, and a person spot-checks its hints for accuracy.

mechanics: Cognitive load theory; scaffolding; expertise-reversal effect
cautions: A fixed schedule leaves some people stranded and bores others. Take support away when you see people succeed, not because the plan says so.
theory: Cognitive load theory; scaffolding; expertise-reversal effect
howTo: Prepare four or five problems of the same type.
Give the first one fully worked. Give the second with the last step left blank.
Remove one more step each time, working backwards from the end.
Check answers after each problem. If most of the room gets one wrong, put a step back.
Finish with a problem that has no help at all.
time: 30 to 45 minutes
group: Alone or in pairs, any group size

name: Expert think-aloud
description: An expert does a real task in front of the group and says out loud what they notice, what they are weighing up and why they choose each move.
bestFor: Reach for it when the skill is mostly judgement, such as diagnosing a fault, reviewing a design or handling a client.

variants.name: Live think-aloud
variants.description: The expert does it in the room, so the group can stop them and ask.

variants.name: Recorded think-aloud
variants.description: The expert records it on video, so you can pause, replay and reuse it.

variants.name: Paired expert think-aloud
variants.description: Two experts do the task together and talk through where they agree and disagree.

variants.name: Think-aloud with learner questioning
variants.description: Learners are told to interrupt with questions at set points.

variants.name: Comparative expert think-aloud
variants.description: Two experts do the same task separately and the group compares how each went about it.

mechanics: Cognitive apprenticeship; modelling; metacognition
cautions: Experts skip the steps they no longer think about, so the most useful parts go unsaid. Stand in for the learner and keep asking why.
theory: Cognitive apprenticeship; modelling; metacognition
howTo: Choose a real task that takes 10 to 15 minutes. Brief the expert to say what they notice and decide, not just what they do.
Give observers a note sheet with three headings: what the expert looked at, what they decided, what they ruled out.
Run the task. When the expert skips something, interrupt with "What made you do that?"
Afterwards, ask pairs to compare notes and list the expert's rules of thumb.
Give learners a similar task and ask them to talk it through to a partner in the same way.
time: 30 to 45 minutes
group: Whole group watching, then pairs, up to 16 people

name: Demonstration then imitation
description: You show the skill being done, then everyone does it themselves while you watch and correct.
bestFor: Reach for it when people need to learn a procedure they do with their hands, a tool or a set way of handling a conversation.

variants.name: Watch-try-feedback
variants.description: The shortest form: one demonstration, one attempt, one piece of feedback, then repeat.

variants.name: I do, we do, you do
variants.description: You show it, then the group does it with you step by step, then each person does it alone.

variants.name: Video modelling then practice
variants.description: The demonstration is a video, which people can replay at their own pace before they practise.

variants.name: Slow-motion demonstration
variants.description: You do each movement or phrase very slowly so nothing is missed.

variants.name: Contrastive demonstration
variants.description: You show a good version and a poor version and ask people to spot the difference.

mechanics: Social learning theory; observational learning; motor learning
cautions: Watching feels like learning, but people cannot do it until they have tried. Keep the demonstration under five minutes and give most of the time to practice with feedback.
theory: Social learning theory; observational learning; motor learning
howTo: Break the skill into three to five steps and name each one.
Show the whole thing once at normal speed, so people see what good looks like.
Show it again slowly. Say the name of each step and the one thing to watch for.
Everyone tries straight away in pairs. One does it and the other checks against the steps.
Walk round and correct one thing per person. Then they do it again.
Finish with one run with no prompts.
time: 20 to 40 minutes
group: Pairs, with up to 12 people per trainer

name: Storytelling and case narrative
description: You teach an idea through a true story: a person, a problem, a decision and what happened next.
bestFor: Reach for it when the topic is culture, ethics or judgement and a list of rules would not stick.

variants.name: Founder story
variants.description: The story of how the organisation began, used to explain what it values.

variants.name: Failure story
variants.description: A story about something that went wrong and what was learnt from it.

variants.name: Customer story
variants.description: A story told from the customer's side of dealing with you.

variants.name: Hero’s journey case
variants.description: The story follows one person who meets a challenge, struggles, gets help and comes back changed.

variants.name: Serialised learning narrative
variants.description: One story runs in episodes across a programme, with a new part in each session.

variants.name: Interactive story circle
variants.description: Each person in a circle tells a two-minute story of their own on the same theme.

mechanics: Narrative cognition; episodic memory; dual coding
cautions: People remember a good story but may take the wrong lesson from it, or only the drama. Always have the group say the point out loud and check it matches yours.
theory: Narrative cognition; episodic memory; dual coding
howTo: Decide the one point the story must make and write it in a sentence.
Pick a true story with a person, a difficulty, a choice and a result. Keep it to three to five minutes.
Tell it up to the moment of decision and stop.
Ask pairs what they would do and why. Take a few answers.
Tell what happened. Then ask the group to state the point in their own words.
Ask each person where the same choice shows up in their own work.
time: 15 to 25 minutes
group: Whole group, with pairs for the discussion

name: Concept mapping
description: Learners draw the ideas in a topic as boxes and join them with labelled arrows that say how one relates to another.
bestFor: Reach for it when people need to see how the parts of a topic or system fit together, or you want to see how they understand it.

variants.name: Individual concept map
variants.description: Each person draws their own, which shows you what each one understands.

variants.name: Collaborative concept map
variants.description: A small group builds one map together and has to agree every link.

variants.name: Causal loop map
variants.description: The arrows show cause and effect, including loops where a result feeds back into its own cause.

variants.name: Journey map
variants.description: The map follows the steps a customer or user goes through over time, with what they do and feel at each one.

variants.name: Knowledge graph exercise
variants.description: Learners link people, systems and documents to show where knowledge sits in the organisation.

variants.name: Before-and-after concept map
variants.description: People draw a map at the start and again at the end, then compare the two.

mechanics: Meaningful learning; schema construction; elaboration
cautions: Maps can look impressive and show little. Make people label every arrow and explain the map aloud, because that is where the gaps show.
theory: Meaningful learning; schema construction; elaboration
howTo: Give a focus question, such as "What affects whether a customer renews?"
Alone, people write 10 to 15 ideas on sticky notes, one per note.
In threes, they arrange the notes on a large sheet and draw arrows between them.
They write a verb or short phrase on every arrow, such as "causes" or "depends on". An arrow with no label does not count.
Each group walks another group through its map in two minutes.
Point out links that are missing or wrong, and let groups revise.
time: 30 to 45 minutes
group: Threes, any group size

name: Deliberate practice
description: Practice aimed at one weak part of a skill. The learner repeats that part against a clear standard, gets corrected each time and tries again.
bestFor: Reach for it when people can do the whole skill roughly and there is a clear picture of what good looks like.

variants.name: Micro-skill isolation drill
variants.description: You practise one tiny piece on its own, such as a single question.

variants.name: Accuracy-first drill
variants.description: People go slowly and get it right before any time pressure is added.

variants.name: Speed-to-fluency drill
variants.description: Once accurate, people repeat against a timer until it comes without effort.

variants.name: Progressive challenge ladder
variants.description: The task gets one step harder each time the learner succeeds.

variants.name: Expert benchmark comparison
variants.description: Learners compare their attempt with an expert's version and list the differences.

variants.name: Immediate-feedback repetition
variants.description: The correction comes straight after each attempt.

variants.name: Delayed-feedback repetition
variants.description: Learners make several attempts and judge them for themselves before any feedback is given.

variants.name: Self-record and review
variants.description: Learners record themselves on a phone and mark the recording against the checklist.

variants.name: Coach-marked repetition
variants.description: A coach scores each attempt against the standard.

variants.name: Criterion-based mastery loop
variants.description: Learners keep repeating until they meet a set standard, such as three clean attempts in a row.

mechanics: Deliberate practice; mental representations; feedback loops
cautions: Repeating something with no standard and no feedback is just repetition, and people get bored. Keep the target small, the standard in view and the feedback quick.
theory: Deliberate practice; mental representations; feedback loops
howTo: Pick one small part of the skill, such as the opening 30 seconds of a sales call.
Show the standard: a model, a checklist of three points or a recording of it done well.
Each person makes a short attempt of one to two minutes.
A coach or partner gives one correction against the standard, straight away.
They repeat at once. Aim for five or more attempts each.
Make it harder only when they hit the standard.
time: 20 to 30 minutes for each part of the skill
group: Pairs or threes, with one coach to about six people

name: Role-play
format: Pairs or groups, live or virtual
description: People act out a work conversation. One practises their own role, another plays the customer or colleague, and an observer gives feedback.
bestFor: Reach for it when people need to practise what to say in sales, feedback, negotiation or customer conversations.

variants.name: Paired role-play
variants.description: Two people only, with no observer, and then they swap.

variants.name: Triad role-play: performer, counterpart, observer
variants.description: Groups of three, where the third person watches against a checklist and gives feedback.

variants.name: Fishbowl role-play
variants.description: One pair plays in the middle while everyone else watches and gives feedback.

variants.name: Rotating-role role-play
variants.description: Everyone takes each role in turn.

variants.name: Reverse-role perspective switch
variants.description: The learner plays the other person, such as the customer, to feel that side of it.

variants.name: Pause-and-coach role-play
variants.description: The coach stops the scene at key moments to give a tip, then it carries on.

variants.name: Rewind-and-retry role-play
variants.description: You go back to the moment it went wrong and play it again a different way.

variants.name: Progressive-difficulty role-play
variants.description: The other person gets harder to deal with each round.

variants.name: Hidden-information role-play
variants.description: The other role holds a fact the learner must uncover by asking good questions.

variants.name: Mystery-stakeholder role-play
variants.description: The learner is not told who they are meeting or what that person wants, and has to work it out in the conversation.

variants.name: Live-actor role-play
variants.description: A trained actor plays the other person, which is more realistic and costs more.

variants.name: Executive-stakeholder role-play
variants.description: The other person is a senior leader with little time and blunt questions.

mechanics: Experiential learning; social learning; behavioural rehearsal
cautions: People dread performing in front of the room, and the other role gets overplayed. Run it in threes with nobody else watching, brief the other role to be realistic, and never skip the second attempt.
theory: Experiential learning; social learning; behavioural rehearsal
howTo: Write a short brief for each role: who you are, what you want and one thing you will push back on.
Put people in threes: one practising, one playing the other person, one observing with a checklist of three behaviours.
Show a two-minute example yourself first, so people know the tone.
Run it for five minutes. The observer then gives feedback for two: one thing that worked and one to change.
The same person goes again straight away with the change.
Rotate roles so everyone practises. Then take the main lessons from the whole group.
time: 40 to 60 minutes
group: Threes, any group size

name: Scenario-based learning
description: Learners read or watch a realistic work situation, decide what to do at each choice point and see what follows from their choice.
bestFor: Reach for it when people face judgement calls where the rules run out, such as ethics, risk or competing priorities.

variants.name: Linear unfolding scenario
variants.description: Everyone follows the same story, which is revealed a stage at a time.

variants.name: Branching scenario
variants.description: Each choice leads to a different next scene, so groups end up in different places.

variants.name: Interactive video scenario
variants.description: The scenes are filmed and the video stops at each choice.

variants.name: Written case scenario
variants.description: The whole thing is on paper, which is cheap and quick to make.

variants.name: Audio scenario
variants.description: Learners listen to a call or meeting and decide what to do next.

variants.name: Live facilitated scenario
variants.description: You read out each stage and run the choices as a group discussion.

variants.name: Competing-priorities scenario
variants.description: Two good aims pull against each other and people must choose.

variants.name: Ethical dilemma scenario
variants.description: The choice is between what is right and what is convenient, or between two duties.

variants.name: Ambiguous-data scenario
variants.description: The information is incomplete or conflicting and people must decide anyway.

variants.name: Role-specific scenario
variants.description: It is written for one job role, with that role's real tasks and terms.

variants.name: Cross-functional scenario
variants.description: People from different teams work the same scenario, each seeing it from their own role.

variants.name: Counterfactual scenario
variants.description: After a real case, people replay it and work out what a different decision would have led to.

mechanics: Situated learning; experiential learning; contextual retrieval
cautions: Tidy scenarios with one obviously right answer teach nothing. Use real cases, make every option tempting and show consequences instead of marking answers right or wrong.
theory: Situated learning; experiential learning; contextual retrieval
howTo: Collect a real situation from the work and leave the mess in: time pressure, missing facts, people who disagree.
Write it in three or four stages. End each stage on a decision with two to four believable options.
People decide alone first and note why.
Small groups compare choices and argue for theirs.
Reveal what happens next for each option, then move to the next stage.
Debrief with "What told you which option was right?" Draw out the cues, not just the answers.
time: 30 to 60 minutes
group: Alone first, then groups of three or four

name: Simulation-based training
description: A safe copy of the real work, such as a mock incident or a practice system, where people can try, fail and try again without real consequences.
bestFor: Reach for it when the real thing is rare, costly or risky, so people cannot learn it on the job.

variants.name: Branching decision simulation
variants.description: The situation changes depending on what the team decides.

variants.name: Escalating scenario simulation
variants.description: Things get worse in stages, so the pressure builds.

variants.name: Timed decision simulation
variants.description: Each decision has a strict time limit.

variants.name: Multi-team simulation
variants.description: Several teams play different parts of the organisation and have to coordinate.

variants.name: Failure-and-recovery simulation
variants.description: Something is set up to go wrong, and the practice is in putting it right.

variants.name: Surprise-inject simulation
variants.description: You drop in unexpected news part way through, such as a system going down.

variants.name: Replay-and-retry simulation
variants.description: Teams run the same simulation twice, with a debrief in between.

variants.name: Live-actor simulation
variants.description: Actors play the customers, patients or stakeholders.

variants.name: Digital-twin simulation
variants.description: The practice runs on a software copy of a real system or process, fed with realistic data.

variants.name: Video-debrief simulation
variants.description: The run is filmed and the debrief uses clips from it.

variants.name: High-fidelity equipment simulation
variants.description: It uses real or near-real kit, such as a flight simulator or a full test environment.

variants.name: Low-fidelity rapid simulation
variants.description: It uses paper, cards and a table, and can be built in an hour.

mechanics: Experiential learning; deliberate practice; representative learning design
cautions: More realism costs more and can swamp beginners with detail. Match the realism to the skill and protect the debrief, because a simulation without one is just an activity.
theory: Experiential learning; deliberate practice; representative learning design
howTo: Decide what people must practise, then build only as much realism as that needs.
Brief people on roles, rules, what is real and what is pretend. Say that mistakes are expected.
Run the simulation for 20 to 40 minutes. Observe and take notes. Do not coach during it.
Debrief for at least as long as the simulation ran: what happened, why, and what to do differently.
Run it again, or run a variation, so people can apply the debrief.
time: 90 minutes to half a day, including the debrief
group: Teams of three to six, with one observer per team

name: AI conversational role-play
description: Learners practise a work conversation by talking or typing with an AI that plays the other person, then get feedback on how it went.
bestFor: Reach for it when people need many repetitions of a conversation and there are not enough partners or coaches to go round.

variants.name: Text-based AI persona
variants.description: The learner types and the AI types back.

variants.name: Voice AI persona
variants.description: The learner speaks and the AI answers aloud, which is closer to a real call.

variants.name: Digital-human avatar role-play
variants.description: The AI appears as an animated face on screen.

variants.name: AI sales prospect
variants.description: The AI plays a possible buyer.

variants.name: AI client stakeholder
variants.description: The AI plays someone on the client side with their own priorities.

variants.name: AI manager conversation
variants.description: The AI plays the learner's manager, for practising speaking upwards.

variants.name: AI employee conversation
variants.description: The AI plays a team member, for practising feedback and one-to-ones.

variants.name: AI negotiation partner
variants.description: The AI bargains against the learner.

variants.name: AI interviewer
variants.description: The AI asks interview questions and follows up on the answers.

variants.name: AI difficult-conversation partner
variants.description: The AI plays someone upset, defensive or angry.

variants.name: AI objection generator
variants.description: The AI fires one objection after another for the learner to answer quickly.

variants.name: Adversarial AI stakeholder
variants.description: The AI is set to be hostile and to resist, for practice late in a programme.

variants.name: Multilingual AI customer
variants.description: The AI plays a customer who speaks another language.

variants.name: AI role-play with human calibration
variants.description: A coach reviews a sample of conversations and corrects the AI's scoring.

mechanics: Behavioural rehearsal; retrieval; adaptive feedback; situated practice
cautions: The AI can give confident feedback that is wrong, can be too agreeable and can carry bias. Have a person check samples, keep real data out and pair it with practice with real people.
theory: Behavioural rehearsal; retrieval; adaptive feedback; situated practice
howTo: Check the tool is approved for your client's data. Tell learners not to enter real names or customer details.
Write the persona: who they are, what they want, how they push back and when they give way.
Test it yourself several times. Fix the brief where the AI is too easy or drifts off.
Give learners a goal and a checklist. Each has two or three conversations of five to ten minutes.
Learners review the transcript against the checklist. Treat the AI's own feedback as a prompt, not a verdict.
Bring the group together to share what worked, and have a trainer or coach review a sample of transcripts.
time: 30 to 45 minutes
group: Individuals, each on their own device, any group size

name: Hands-on lab
description: Learners carry out set tasks in the real tool, or in a safe practice copy of it, with realistic data.
bestFor: Reach for it when people need to be able to use a product, system or process, not just know about it.

variants.name: Guided recipe lab
variants.description: Every step is written out, for a first contact with the tool.

variants.name: Troubleshooting lab
variants.description: The environment has faults planted in it for learners to find and fix.

variants.name: Sandbox exploration lab
variants.description: Learners get a safe copy and a goal, and find their own way.

variants.name: Challenge lab
variants.description: Learners get a result to reach and no steps.

variants.name: Build-and-break lab
variants.description: Learners build something, break it on purpose and then repair it.

variants.name: Pair lab
variants.description: Two people share one screen, one doing and one directing, and then swap.

variants.name: Open lab with expert office hours
variants.description: Learners work in their own time and an expert is on hand at set hours.

variants.name: Timed lab
variants.description: The tasks are done against the clock.

variants.name: Cross-tool integration lab
variants.description: The task needs two or more tools working together.

variants.name: Production-like lab
variants.description: The practice environment mirrors the live one, with realistic data and volumes.

mechanics: Learning by doing; cognitive apprenticeship; immediate feedback
cautions: People follow the steps and finish without understanding, so take the steps away as the lab goes on and add a fault to find. Setup problems eat the session, so test logins and data the day before.
theory: Learning by doing; cognitive apprenticeship; immediate feedback
howTo: Set up a practice environment and test every step on a learner's login, not your own.
Give a task sheet that states the result to reach. Give click-by-click steps for the first task only.
Demonstrate the first task in five minutes.
People work alone or in pairs while you walk round. Ask them to try for two minutes before they call you.
Include one task where something is broken and they must find out why.
Close with a task from their own work, done with no instructions.
time: 45 to 90 minutes
group: Alone or in pairs, with up to 12 people per trainer

name: Practice clinic
description: A small group where each person brings a real piece of work, performs it, gets feedback from a coach and the group, and tries again.
bestFor: Reach for it when people are working on presenting, facilitating, pitching or leading and have something real coming up.

variants.name: Pitch clinic
variants.description: People practise a sales or funding pitch.

variants.name: Facilitation clinic
variants.description: People practise running a short group activity.

variants.name: Storytelling clinic
variants.description: People practise telling a work story to make a point.

variants.name: Negotiation clinic
variants.description: People practise a negotiation they have coming up.

variants.name: Coaching clinic
variants.description: People practise coaching a colleague and get feedback on their questions.

variants.name: Prompt clinic
variants.description: People bring prompts they have written for an AI tool and improve them together.

variants.name: Design critique clinic
variants.description: People bring a design in progress for review against agreed standards.

variants.name: Executive presence clinic
variants.description: People practise how they come across to senior audiences: voice, pace and brevity.

variants.name: Technical troubleshooting clinic
variants.description: People bring a real technical fault and talk through how they would diagnose it.

variants.name: Client discovery clinic
variants.description: People practise a first client meeting, where they ask questions to find out what the client needs.

mechanics: Deliberate practice; peer learning; feedback literacy
cautions: Without an agreed standard the feedback turns into personal taste, and time runs out before the last people have a turn. Fix the criteria and the time per person at the start.
theory: Deliberate practice; peer learning; feedback literacy
howTo: Ask each person to bring something real and short, such as the opening of a talk they will give.
Agree the standard first: three or four things you are all looking for.
One person performs for three to five minutes.
Give feedback for five minutes against the standard. The performer speaks first, then peers, then the coach.
The performer repeats the part that needs work, straight away.
Move to the next person. Allow about 15 minutes each.
time: 15 minutes a person, so about 90 minutes for six people
group: Four to six people per coach

name: Mock assessment centre
description: A practice run of an assessment day. Learners do several work-like exercises while trained observers score them against set criteria, then get feedback.
bestFor: Reach for it when people are preparing for promotion or a bigger role and want an honest picture of their strengths and gaps.
mechanics: Behavioural observation; simulation; criterion-referenced assessment
cautions: If it feels like a real test, people play safe and learn less, and observers who mark differently make the feedback unfair. Say plainly that it is for development and that scores go no further, and train the observers together.
theory: Behavioural observation; simulation; criterion-referenced assessment
howTo: Choose three or four behaviours to assess. Write what good looks like for each.
Pick three exercises, such as a group discussion, a role-play and a short presentation.
Brief the observers together and score one example jointly, so they mark alike.
Run the exercises in rotation, 20 to 30 minutes each, with one observer to two learners.
Observers write down what they saw and heard first, and score second.
Give each person a 20-minute feedback talk with two strengths and two things to work on.
time: Half a day to a full day
group: 6 to 12 learners, with three to six observers

name: Teach-back
description: After you have taught something, learners explain or show it back to a partner in their own words, with notes closed.
bestFor: Reach for it when you want to check what people have understood and make them recall it.

variants.name: One-minute teach-back
variants.description: Each explanation is held to 60 seconds.

variants.name: Peer teach-back
variants.description: Learners explain to each other in pairs, not to the trainer.

variants.name: Client-language teach-back
variants.description: Learners explain it as they would to a client, with no internal jargon.

variants.name: Reverse teach-back
variants.description: You explain it back with planted mistakes, and learners catch and correct them.

variants.name: Demonstration teach-back
variants.description: Learners show the skill being done while they explain it.

mechanics: Retrieval practice; elaboration; generation effect
cautions: Partners can pass on mistakes with confidence. Listen in as they talk and always finish with a correct version from you.
theory: Retrieval practice; elaboration; generation effect
howTo: Teach a chunk of 10 to 15 minutes.
Ask everyone to close their notes and take a minute to think.
In pairs, A explains it to B for two minutes, as if B had missed the session.
B says what was missing or unclear. Then they swap, on a different part.
Take two or three explanations from the room and correct any errors in front of everyone.
time: 5 to 10 minutes a round
group: Pairs, any group size

name: Peer instruction
description: You ask a hard multiple-choice question. Everyone votes alone, then argues their answer with a neighbour, then votes again.
bestFor: Reach for it when the topic has ideas that people commonly get wrong.

variants.name: Concept-test peer instruction
variants.description: The classic form, with a short question that tests one idea.

variants.name: Prediction-discussion-revote
variants.description: People predict what a demonstration will show, discuss, vote again and then watch it.

variants.name: Case-vote peer instruction
variants.description: The question is a short case and people vote on what to do.

variants.name: Confidence-rated peer instruction
variants.description: People also rate how sure they are, which shows up confident wrong answers.

variants.name: Peer instruction with expert reveal
variants.description: An expert gives their answer and reasoning after the second vote.

mechanics: Retrieval; elaboration; cognitive conflict; social constructivism
cautions: Easy questions produce no debate, and a majority vote can still be wrong. Write questions around real misunderstandings and always explain the answer yourself.
theory: Retrieval; elaboration; cognitive conflict; social constructivism
howTo: Write a multiple-choice question where the wrong options are the mistakes people really make.
Everyone answers alone with no talking, by poll or by holding up cards.
Look at the spread. If nearly everyone is right, move on. If very few are, teach it again. If it is split, carry on.
Tell people to find someone who answered differently and convince them. Give two to three minutes.
Vote again.
Reveal the answer and explain why each wrong option is wrong.
time: 8 to 12 minutes a question
group: Pairs, from 8 people to several hundred

name: Learning by teaching
description: Learners prepare and teach a short session on part of the topic to other people. Getting ready to teach makes them organise the material and expect questions.
bestFor: Reach for it near the end of a programme, when you want people to pull a topic together.

variants.name: Mini-masterclass
variants.description: One learner teaches the group for 10 minutes on something they know well.

variants.name: Learner-created tutorial
variants.description: Learners write a short how-to guide for others to use.

variants.name: Peer explainer video
variants.description: Learners record a video of two to three minutes that explains one idea.

variants.name: Teach-the-next-cohort
variants.description: People who have finished the programme teach part of it to the next group.

variants.name: Public demonstration
variants.description: Learners show the skill to an audience outside the group, such as their own team.

mechanics: Generative learning; retrieval; metacognition
cautions: People can teach something wrong with great confidence, and the audience believes them. Check the plans beforehand and correct errors in front of the audience.
theory: Generative learning; retrieval; metacognition
howTo: Give each pair or three a different part of the topic and a real audience, such as the rest of the group.
Allow 20 to 30 minutes to prepare a session of five to eight minutes, with one example and one question for the audience.
Ask each team to write down three questions they expect to be asked.
Check each team's plan before they teach.
Each team teaches and takes questions from the audience.
Straight after each one, correct anything wrong and add what was missed.
time: 60 to 90 minutes
group: Pairs or threes teaching a group of 8 to 16

name: Problem-based learning
description: Small groups start with a messy, real problem before any teaching. They work out what they need to know, find it out and come back with a response.
bestFor: Reach for it when people already have the basics and need to combine them and reason the way practitioners do.

variants.name: Single-problem tutorial
variants.description: One problem, worked through in one or two sessions with a tutor.

variants.name: Progressive problem sequence
variants.description: A series of problems, each harder than the last and building on it.

variants.name: Cross-functional problem lab
variants.description: Each group mixes people from different departments.

variants.name: Client problem clinic
variants.description: The problem comes from a real client, with that client's limits and people.

variants.name: Policy problem lab
variants.description: The problem is how to write or apply a policy or rule.

variants.name: Diagnostic problem lab
variants.description: The task is to find the cause of a fault or a poor result.

variants.name: Data-rich problem lab
variants.description: Groups get real data sets to analyse as part of the problem.

variants.name: Constraint-based problem
variants.description: The problem comes with tight limits on budget, time or tools.

mechanics: Constructivism; self-directed learning; situated cognition
cautions: Beginners flounder if they lack the basic knowledge. Teach the foundations first, or give more structure, such as guiding questions and a reading list.
theory: Constructivism; self-directed learning; situated cognition
howTo: Write a one-page problem from real work that has no single right answer.
In groups of four to six, people list what they know, what they do not know and what they need to find out.
They split the research and go and find out. Allow 30 minutes in a session, or a few days between sessions.
They come back, share what they found and agree a response.
Each group presents its response and its reasoning. You question the reasoning.
Close by naming what was learnt and what is still open.
time: Two to three hours in one session, or spread over two sessions
group: Groups of four to six, with a tutor checking in on each

name: Project-based learning
format: Team project over days or weeks
description: Learners build something substantial and real over days or weeks, alone or in teams, and learn what they need along the way.
bestFor: Reach for it when people need to combine several skills and finish with evidence of what they can do.

variants.name: Individual capstone project
variants.description: One person does a final project that pulls the whole programme together.

variants.name: Team capstone project
variants.description: A team does the final project together.

variants.name: Client-sponsored project
variants.description: A real client sets the brief and receives the result.

variants.name: Prototype project
variants.description: The output is a working first version of a product or service.

variants.name: Research-to-recommendation project
variants.description: Learners research a question and present a recommendation to the people who decide.

variants.name: Implementation project
variants.description: Learners put a change into practice in their own workplace.

variants.name: Portfolio project
variants.description: The output joins a collection of work the learner can show as evidence of skill.

variants.name: Community-impact project
variants.description: The project is done for a charity or a local community group.

variants.name: Cross-functional build project
variants.description: People from different departments build something together.

variants.name: Thirty-day applied project
variants.description: A project fixed at 30 days and done alongside the normal job.

mechanics: Situated learning; constructionism; experiential learning
cautions: One or two people can carry a team, and a polished output can hide weak basics. Check each person's contribution and test the key skills separately.
theory: Situated learning; constructionism; experiential learning
howTo: Set a brief with a real output, a real audience and clear criteria.
Agree milestones, such as a plan, a first draft and a final version, with a review at each.
Teach short inputs when the project needs them, not all at the start.
At each milestone, give feedback against the criteria and have teams review each other.
End with a presentation to the real audience.
Ask each person to write what they contributed and what they learnt.
time: Two to eight weeks, at a few hours a week
group: Alone, or teams of three to five

name: Challenge-based learning
description: Teams take on a broad real-world challenge set with someone outside the group. They investigate it, try something in practice and report what changed.
bestFor: Reach for it when you want people from different teams to work together on something that matters to the organisation.

variants.name: Executive-sponsored challenge
variants.description: A senior leader sets the challenge and hears the results.

variants.name: Social-impact challenge
variants.description: The challenge is a social problem, often worked on with a charity.

variants.name: Innovation challenge
variants.description: The task is to come up with and test a new product, service or way of working.

variants.name: Sustainability challenge
variants.description: The task is to cut waste, energy use or carbon.

variants.name: AI adoption challenge
variants.description: Teams find and test a real use for AI tools in their own work.

variants.name: Customer-experience challenge
variants.description: The task is to fix a point where customers struggle.

variants.name: Process-redesign challenge
variants.description: The task is to make an internal process simpler or faster.

variants.name: Grand challenge tournament
variants.description: Many teams take on the same challenge and the best responses are chosen in rounds.

mechanics: Experiential learning; inquiry; authentic assessment
cautions: A vague challenge produces slides and then nothing changes. Tie the challenge down, and get a named owner for the follow-up before you start.
theory: Experiential learning; inquiry; authentic assessment
howTo: Agree the challenge with a sponsor who will act on the results. Narrow it to a question a team can do something about in the time.
Teams investigate first. They talk to the people affected and gather facts.
Each team picks one thing to try and a way to tell if it worked.
They try it for real, on a small scale.
Teams present what they did, what the evidence shows and what should happen next.
The sponsor says on the day what will be taken forward and who owns it.
time: Two to six weeks, or two full days in a compressed form
group: Teams of four to six

name: Case method
description: Learners read a written account of a real situation, decide what they would do and defend that decision in a discussion you lead.
bestFor: Reach for it when people need to practise business judgement and trade-offs where no rule gives the answer.

variants.name: Decision-forcing case
variants.description: The case stops at the decision, and learners must choose before they hear what happened.

variants.name: Comparative cases
variants.description: Two cases are read together to find what explains the different results.

variants.name: Mini-case
variants.description: A case of half a page, read in the room and discussed in 15 minutes.

variants.name: Multimedia case
variants.description: The case comes as video, audio and documents instead of plain text.

variants.name: Live case discussion
variants.description: Someone who was involved in the case joins the discussion and answers questions.

variants.name: Cold-call case seminar
variants.description: You pick people to speak without warning, so everyone has to prepare.

variants.name: Case debate
variants.description: Two teams are given opposite sides and argue them.

variants.name: Case jigsaw
variants.description: Each group gets a different part of the case and they must pool what they know.

variants.name: Case reconstruction
variants.description: Learners get the outcome and work backwards to how it came about.

variants.name: Case sequel
variants.description: After the discussion, learners get a follow-up that shows what happened next, and decide again.

mechanics: Situated cognition; elaboration; decision practice
cautions: Cases reward confident talkers and look tidier in hindsight than they were. Call on quiet people, and ask what the people in the case could have known at the time.
theory: Situated cognition; elaboration; decision practice
howTo: Choose a case that ends at a decision. Send it ahead with two or three questions.
Open with a vote: "What would you do?"
Ask one person to argue their choice, then someone who disagrees.
Keep asking "Why?" and "What would have to be true for that to work?" Write the arguments on the board in two columns.
Hold back your own view until late.
Close by saying what happened, if it is known, and asking what principles the group will take away.
time: 45 to 75 minutes, plus reading beforehand
group: Whole group of 8 to 30, with small groups for preparation

name: Live case
description: A real organisation brings a current problem it has not solved. Its sponsor briefs the learners, who work on it and present recommendations or a prototype back.
bestFor: Reach for it with experienced learners when a sponsor has a real problem and intends to use what they produce.

variants.name: Internal business live case
variants.description: The problem comes from the learners' own organisation.

variants.name: External client live case
variants.description: The problem comes from a client or partner organisation.

variants.name: Non-profit live case
variants.description: The problem comes from a charity.

variants.name: Executive dilemma live case
variants.description: A senior leader brings a decision they are facing now.

variants.name: Operational live case
variants.description: The problem is in day-to-day operations, such as delays or errors.

variants.name: Transformation live case
variants.description: The problem is part of a large change programme.

variants.name: Data-backed live case
variants.description: The sponsor supplies real data for teams to analyse.

variants.name: Live case with stakeholder jury
variants.description: A panel of the people affected judges the recommendations.

mechanics: Authentic learning; situated cognition; transfer
cautions: If the sponsor is not ready to use the results it becomes an exercise, and learners notice. Confirm the sponsor's commitment and the confidentiality terms before the programme starts.
theory: Authentic learning; situated cognition; transfer
howTo: Find a sponsor with a real, open problem and agree what they will do with the results.
Agree confidentiality and what data learners can see.
The sponsor briefs the group for 30 minutes and takes questions.
Teams work on it, with one chance to check back with the sponsor part way through.
Teams present to the sponsor, who gives frank feedback.
Debrief the learning separately from the result: what skills people used and what they would do differently.
time: One day to several weeks
group: Teams of four to six

name: Design sprint
description: A team works through a fixed sequence in a short, timed burst: understand the problem, sketch ideas, choose one, build a rough version and test it with real users.
bestFor: Reach for it when a team has a real product or service problem and you want them to learn the design process by doing it.

variants.name: Two-hour lightning sprint
variants.description: A taster that runs each stage in 15 to 20 minutes and tests on colleagues.

variants.name: One-day design sprint
variants.description: All the stages in one day, with a paper prototype.

variants.name: Three-day sprint
variants.description: A day to understand and sketch, a day to decide and build, and a day to test.

variants.name: Five-day sprint (Google Ventures format)
variants.description: The original format from Google Ventures, with one stage a day from Monday to Friday.

variants.name: Remote design sprint
variants.description: Run on video calls and an online whiteboard, usually in shorter sessions over more days.

variants.name: Service design sprint
variants.description: The thing being designed is a service or process, not a screen.

variants.name: AI-assisted sprint
variants.description: The team uses AI tools to produce ideas, copy or prototypes faster, and checks the output itself.

variants.name: Inclusive design sprint
variants.description: The team designs and tests with people who are often left out, such as disabled users.

tierRaw: D/B - Practitioner framework with supporting mechanisms
mechanics: Design thinking; experiential learning; rapid feedback
cautions: The pace can squeeze out proper research, and often nothing gets built afterwards. Say who owns the next step before you start, and treat it as a way of working on a problem, not a general teaching method.
theory: Design thinking; experiential learning; rapid feedback
howTo: Set the challenge and book five test users before you start.
Understand: map the problem and pick one part to focus on.
Sketch: everyone draws their own solution alone, in silence.
Decide: put the sketches on the wall, vote with dots, and have one named person make the final call.
Prototype: build something just real enough to test.
Test: show it to the users one at a time, watch, and note what works and what does not.
time: One to five days, or two hours for a taster
group: One team of five to seven, with a facilitator

name: Hackathon / buildathon
description: Teams have a fixed, short time, often a day or two, to build a working solution to a problem and show it at the end.
bestFor: Reach for it when you want people to apply new technical skills quickly and mix with people from other teams.

variants.name: Technical hackathon
variants.description: Teams write code.

variants.name: No-code buildathon
variants.description: Teams build with tools that need no coding, so anyone can take part.

variants.name: AI hackathon
variants.description: Teams build something with AI tools, inside agreed rules on what data may be used.

variants.name: Data hackathon
variants.description: Teams get a data set and a question to answer.

variants.name: Design hackathon
variants.description: Teams produce designs and prototypes, not code.

variants.name: Policy hackathon
variants.description: Teams draft a policy or proposal.

variants.name: Internal process hackathon
variants.description: Teams fix a process inside the organisation.

variants.name: Client co-creation hackathon
variants.description: Client staff join the teams and build alongside them.

variants.name: Prototype marathon
variants.description: A longer event where the aim is a prototype ready to test.

variants.name: Mini-hack sprint
variants.description: A version of two to three hours that fits inside a workshop.

mechanics: Constructionism; flow; social learning; authentic practice
cautions: It rewards speed over quality, wears people out and can leave beginners watching. Mix teams on purpose, give beginners a real job, build in breaks and avoid overnight formats.
theory: Constructionism; flow; social learning; authentic practice
howTo: Set a theme and judging criteria. Include what was learnt, not just polish.
Form teams of three to five that mix skills and experience.
Open with the brief, the rules and the tools, then start the clock.
Have mentors circulate, and hold a short check-in every few hours.
Each team gives a three-minute demo of something that works.
Judge against the criteria. Then debrief what people learnt and say what happens to the builds.
time: One to two days, or three hours for a mini version
group: Teams of three to five, from 12 to 100 or more people

name: Innovation tournament
description: A group produces a large number of ideas, then cuts them down in rounds against stated criteria. The few that are left get developed further.
bestFor: Reach for it when an organisation wants to choose which ideas to back and to show people how to judge ideas on evidence.

variants.name: Open idea tournament
variants.description: Anyone in the organisation can submit an idea.

variants.name: Evidence-gated tournament
variants.description: An idea only moves to the next round with evidence, such as a test with customers.

variants.name: Shark-tank pitch
variants.description: Finalists pitch live to a panel that decides on the spot.

variants.name: Crowd-ranked tournament
variants.description: Everyone votes to rank the ideas.

variants.name: Expert-jury tournament
variants.description: A panel of experts makes the cuts.

mechanics: Variation-selection theory; decision science; collective intelligence
cautions: Criteria and voters favour familiar ideas, and popular is not the same as good. Ask for evidence at every round, and treat this as a way of choosing ideas, because it builds little skill by itself.
theory: Variation-selection theory; decision science; collective intelligence
howTo: State the question and publish the criteria before anyone submits.
Round one: everyone submits ideas of a few lines each. Aim for a lot of them.
Round two: people score the ideas against the criteria and the top quarter go through.
Round three: small teams develop each surviving idea with evidence, such as a customer conversation or a rough cost.
Final: teams pitch for five minutes and a panel picks what goes forward.
Tell everyone what was chosen and why.
time: Half a day in a workshop, or four to six weeks across an organisation
group: From 12 people to a whole organisation

name: Studio learning / design critique
description: Learners work on their own piece, put the unfinished work on show and get feedback on it from peers and a tutor against agreed standards.
bestFor: Reach for it when the skill is judged by the quality of what people make, as in design, writing or strategy.

variants.name: Pin-up critique
variants.description: Everyone's work goes on the wall and is discussed one piece at a time.

variants.name: Desk critique
variants.description: The tutor goes from desk to desk and gives feedback one to one.

variants.name: Gallery critique
variants.description: People walk round the displayed work and leave written comments on sticky notes.

variants.name: Expert jury critique
variants.description: Outside experts review the finished work.

variants.name: Peer critique circle
variants.description: A small group of peers reviews each other's work with no tutor.

variants.name: Open studio
variants.description: People work in a shared space and ask for feedback when they want it.

variants.name: Masterclass studio
variants.description: An expert reworks one learner's piece in front of the group.

variants.name: Atelier apprenticeship
variants.description: Learners spend a long period in an expert's studio, working on the expert's real projects.

variants.name: Work-in-progress review
variants.description: A regular short slot where people show unfinished work early.

variants.name: Public demo critique
variants.description: Work is shown to an outside audience, who give feedback.

mechanics: Situated learning; cognitive apprenticeship; feedback literacy
cautions: Feedback can turn personal, or stay vague and polite. Talk about the work and not the person, tie each comment to a standard, and model it yourself first.
theory: Situated learning; cognitive apprenticeship; feedback literacy
howTo: Set a brief and state the standards the work will be judged against.
People work on it, in the session or beforehand.
Each person pins up their work and takes two minutes to say what they were aiming for and where they want feedback.
The group responds for five to eight minutes: what works, what does not and why, tied to the standards.
The maker listens and takes notes without defending the work.
Everyone revises, and shows the change at the next session.
time: 10 to 15 minutes a person, so about 90 minutes for six people
group: Four to eight people

name: Escape-room learning
description: Teams solve a chain of puzzles against the clock to get through a story. Each puzzle needs something from the training content to solve it.
bestFor: Reach for it when you want people to revise content and want to see how a team works together under time pressure.

variants.name: Physical escape room
variants.description: A real room with locks, props and hidden clues.

variants.name: Portable escape box
variants.description: The puzzles are in a locked box you can carry to any venue.

variants.name: Digital escape room
variants.description: It is played on screen, in the room or remotely.

variants.name: Cybersecurity escape room
variants.description: The puzzles are about spotting and stopping security threats.

variants.name: Compliance escape room
variants.description: The puzzles test rules and policy.

variants.name: Process escape room
variants.description: The puzzles follow the steps of a work process.

variants.name: Teamwork escape room
variants.description: It is built so nobody can solve it alone, and the debrief is about how the team worked.

variants.name: Knowledge-retrieval escape room
variants.description: Every puzzle is a recall question on content taught earlier.

mechanics: Game-based learning; retrieval; collaborative problem solving
cautions: The game can be all that people remember, and the fastest person can solve everything. Make sure every puzzle needs the content, and do not skip the debrief.
theory: Game-based learning; retrieval; collaborative problem solving
howTo: List five or six things people must recall or apply. Write one puzzle for each.
Chain them so each answer opens the next, with a simple story on top.
Test it on colleagues and time it. Fix any puzzle that needs luck or outside knowledge.
Run it in teams of four or five, with a visible clock and up to three hints.
Debrief for 15 to 20 minutes: which content was hard, and how the team worked.
time: 30 to 45 minutes of play, plus 20 minutes of debrief
group: Teams of four or five

name: Cohort-based course
description: A fixed group starts and finishes a multi-week course together, with set dates, live sessions, tasks in between and each other for support.
bestFor: Reach for it when the skill takes weeks to build, such as moving into a new role, and people gain from knowing each other.

variants.name: Synchronous cohort
variants.description: Everyone meets live at the same time for every session.

variants.name: Hybrid cohort
variants.description: Some sessions are in person and some are online.

variants.name: Peer-led cohort
variants.description: Members take turns to run the sessions, with no expert.

variants.name: Role-based cohort
variants.description: Everyone has the same job role.

variants.name: Cross-functional cohort
variants.description: People come from different departments.

variants.name: Executive cohort
variants.description: A cohort for senior leaders, usually smaller and with more confidentiality.

variants.name: Global follow-the-sun cohort
variants.description: The same session runs at several times of day, so each time zone can join in working hours.

variants.name: Cohort with local pods
variants.description: The course is online and small local groups also meet in person.

variants.name: Cohort with live residency
variants.description: The course includes a few days together in one place.

variants.name: Cohort with workplace capstone
variants.description: The course ends with a project done in the learner's own job.

mechanics: Social learning; accountability; communities of practice
cautions: Fixed dates shut out people who cannot make them, and energy dips in the middle weeks. Record what you can, keep the small groups going, and do not assume the group format alone is why people finish.
theory: Social learning; accountability; communities of practice
howTo: Fix the group and the dates, say six weeks with one live session a week.
Start with a session that helps people get to know each other and agree how they will work together.
Set a task between sessions that people apply at work and bring back.
Put people in small groups of three or four that meet between sessions.
Open every session with what people tried since the last one.
End with each person showing something they made or did.
time: Four to twelve weeks, at two to four hours a week
group: 12 to 30 people, in small groups of three or four

name: Community of practice
description: A standing group of people who do the same kind of work and meet regularly to share cases, tools and problems, so they all get better at it.
bestFor: Reach for it when learning has to carry on after a course ends and knowledge needs to move between teams.

variants.name: Craft guild
variants.description: People who share a skill, such as writing or facilitation, across the whole organisation.

variants.name: Role community
variants.description: People who hold the same job.

variants.name: Practice circle
variants.description: A small group that meets to rehearse a skill together.

variants.name: Technical community
variants.description: People who work with the same technology.

variants.name: Leadership community
variants.description: Managers who share people problems in confidence.

variants.name: Client case community
variants.description: Members bring client situations, with names removed, to work through together.

variants.name: Local chapter network
variants.description: Local groups meet in person and link up now and then.

variants.name: Global community with market chapters
variants.description: One community across countries, with a sub-group for each market.

variants.name: Community challenge cycle
variants.description: The community sets itself a shared challenge each quarter and shows the results.

variants.name: Community knowledge exchange
variants.description: Meetings where members swap tools and methods that have worked for them.

mechanics: Situated learning; legitimate peripheral participation
cautions: Communities fade without someone looking after them and real work to do. Give the organisers time for it and build every meeting around a real problem.
theory: Situated learning; legitimate peripheral participation
howTo: Name the craft and who the group is for. Find two or three keen people to run it.
Set a rhythm, such as an hour a month.
Give each meeting a fixed shape: one member brings a real case, the group works on it, then a round of quick tips.
Keep a shared place for useful templates and notes.
Ask members every few months what is useful and what to drop.
time: An hour a month, ongoing
group: 8 to 40 members, with two or three organisers

name: Cognitive apprenticeship
description: An expert teaches a thinking skill the way a craft is taught. They show it while talking through their reasoning, coach the learner through it, then step back bit by bit.
bestFor: Reach for it when the skill is complex professional judgement that experts use without finding it easy to explain.

variants.name: Model-coach-fade cycle
variants.description: The short form: show it, coach it, then pull the help away.

variants.name: Guided participation
variants.description: The learner joins real work in a small role and the expert steers as they go.

variants.name: Expert shadow plus articulation
variants.description: The learner shadows the expert, who stops at intervals to explain what they were thinking.

variants.name: Apprentice studio
variants.description: Several learners work alongside one expert in a shared space.

variants.name: Remote cognitive apprenticeship
variants.description: It is done by screen share and recorded walk-throughs.

mechanics: Cognitive apprenticeship; situated cognition
cautions: It takes a lot of expert time, and many experts struggle to put their thinking into words. Train the experts to think aloud and make room for it in their workload.
theory: Cognitive apprenticeship; situated cognition
howTo: Model: the expert does a real task and says their thinking out loud.
Coach: the learner does a similar task while the expert watches and gives hints.
Support: give aids such as a checklist, and take them away as the learner improves.
Explain: ask the learner to talk through their own reasoning while they work.
Compare: the learner sets their work beside the expert's and names the differences.
Release: the learner takes on whole tasks alone and brings back only the hard parts.
time: Weeks to months, in sessions of 30 to 60 minutes
group: One expert with one to four learners

name: Mentoring
description: A more experienced person meets a less experienced one over months to share what they know, open doors and help them think about their career.
bestFor: Reach for it when someone needs help with career growth, contacts and how the organisation really works.

variants.name: Traditional senior-junior mentoring
variants.description: A senior person mentors a junior one.

variants.name: Reverse mentoring
variants.description: A junior person mentors a senior one, often on technology or on what work is like lower down.

variants.name: Reciprocal mentoring
variants.description: Both people mentor each other on different things.

variants.name: Group mentoring
variants.description: One mentor meets several mentees together.

variants.name: Peer mentoring
variants.description: Two people at the same level mentor each other.

variants.name: Flash mentoring
variants.description: A single conversation on one question.

variants.name: Speed mentoring
variants.description: A room of mentors and mentees swap partners every 10 minutes.

variants.name: Mentoring circles
variants.description: A small group meets regularly with one or two mentors.

variants.name: Sponsor-backed mentoring
variants.description: The senior person also speaks up for the mentee when jobs and projects are handed out.

variants.name: Cross-functional mentoring
variants.description: The mentor comes from a different department.

mechanics: Social learning; possible selves; developmental relationships
cautions: Poor matches, unclear aims and a mentor who is also the mentee's manager all weaken it. Match with care, agree goals at the first meeting and choose mentors from outside the mentee's reporting line.
theory: Social learning; possible selves; developmental relationships
howTo: Match on what the mentee wants to learn, and let both sides say no.
Hold a first meeting to agree goals, how often to meet, confidentiality and an end date.
Meet for about an hour a month. The mentee sets the agenda and sends it ahead.
The mentor shares experience and contacts, and asks questions before giving advice.
Review at the halfway point whether it is working.
End on purpose. Look back at the goals and close, or agree a new term.
time: An hour a month for six to twelve months
group: One to one, or one mentor with three to five mentees

name: Coaching
description: A coach works with one person or a small group on a goal they choose. The coach watches, asks questions, challenges and helps them plan things to try between sessions.
bestFor: Reach for it when someone wants to change how they behave at work or sharpen a skill they already have.

variants.name: Executive coaching
variants.description: For senior leaders, usually with an outside coach.

variants.name: Skills coaching
variants.description: Aimed at one specific skill, such as presenting.

variants.name: Performance coaching
variants.description: Aimed at results in the current job.

variants.name: Team coaching
variants.description: A whole team is coached together on how it works.

variants.name: Group coaching
variants.description: Several people with separate goals are coached in one group.

variants.name: Manager-as-coach
variants.description: The line manager coaches as part of normal one-to-ones.

variants.name: Observational coaching
variants.description: The coach watches the person at work and gives feedback afterwards.

variants.name: Solution-focused coaching
variants.description: The talk centres on what already works and the next small step, not on the causes of the problem.

variants.name: Strengths-based coaching
variants.description: The coach builds on what the person does well.

variants.name: Domain-expert coaching
variants.description: The coach is an expert in the subject and gives advice as well as asking questions.

mechanics: Self-regulation; goal-setting; feedback; deliberate practice
cautions: Questions alone do not help someone who lacks the knowledge, and coaching cannot fix a broken process or a bad manager. Check the cause first, and bring in someone who knows the subject when knowledge is the gap.
theory: Self-regulation; goal-setting; feedback; deliberate practice
howTo: Agree a goal the person cares about, and how you will both know it has moved.
Where you can, watch them at work or look at real evidence.
In each session, ask what they tried, what happened and what they make of it.
Help them choose one small thing to try before next time.
Start the next session with how that went.
Review against the goal every three or four sessions.
time: 45 to 60 minutes every two to four weeks, for three to six months
group: One to one, or groups of four to six

name: Peer coaching
description: Colleagues at the same level coach each other in pairs or threes, following a set list of questions.
bestFor: Reach for it when you want everyone on a programme to keep applying what they learnt and there is no budget for professional coaches.

variants.name: Coaching pairs
variants.description: Two people coach each other in turn.

variants.name: Coaching triads
variants.description: Three people rotate as coach, person being coached and observer.

variants.name: Rotating peer coaches
variants.description: Partners change every few sessions.

variants.name: Accountability partners
variants.description: A short weekly check-in on what each person committed to.

variants.name: Peer observation coaching
variants.description: Peers watch each other at work and give feedback.

variants.name: Case-based peer coaching
variants.description: One person brings a real case and the others coach them on it.

variants.name: Remote peer coaching
variants.description: It is done by video call.

variants.name: Cross-role peer coaching
variants.description: The partner comes from a different job or team.

mechanics: Social learning; self-regulation; reflective practice
cautions: Without a structure it becomes a chat or a round of advice. Give the question card, practise once in the room, and say where to take problems that are too big for a peer.
theory: Social learning; self-regulation; reflective practice
howTo: Teach a simple structure: the goal, what happened, what you will try next.
Give a card with five or six questions and one rule: no advice until the person asks for it.
Agree ground rules: confidentiality, equal time, and what to pass on to someone else.
Run 20 minutes per person, with a timekeeper.
End each session with one written commitment each.
Start the next session with how that went.
time: 40 to 60 minutes a session, every two to four weeks
group: Pairs or threes, any group size

name: Action learning sets
description: A small group meets regularly. Each member brings a real problem, the others help by asking questions instead of advising, and the member commits to an action and reports back.
bestFor: Reach for it with leaders or cross-team groups who have real problems with no known answer.

variants.name: Classic Revans set
variants.description: The original form from Reg Revans, with peers questioning each other and no expert teaching.

variants.name: Leadership action learning set
variants.description: All the members are managers working on leadership problems.

variants.name: Cross-functional set
variants.description: The members come from different departments.

variants.name: Client challenge set
variants.description: The problems are about real clients.

variants.name: Virtual action learning set
variants.description: The set meets by video call.

variants.name: Rapid action learning sprint
variants.description: A compressed version inside a workshop, with 20 minutes per problem.

variants.name: Action learning with sponsor reviews
variants.description: A senior sponsor hears progress at set points.

mechanics: Action learning; experiential learning; reflective practice
cautions: It drifts into advice-giving, or into talk with no action. Hold the questions-only rule firmly and start every meeting with the action reports.
theory: Action learning; experiential learning; reflective practice
howTo: Form a set of five to seven people who do not report to each other. Agree confidentiality.
One person presents a problem for five minutes.
The others ask open questions for 15 to 20 minutes. No advice and no stories of their own.
The presenter says what they now see and names one action.
Repeat for two or three presenters in a session.
Open the next meeting with reports on those actions.
time: Two to three hours, every four to six weeks, for six months or more
group: Sets of five to seven

name: World Café
description: People sit at small tables to discuss a question, then move to new tables for further rounds. A host stays at each table to pass on what was said before.
bestFor: Reach for it when a large group needs to share views, meet each other and find common themes.

variants.name: Classic rotating World Café
variants.description: The standard form, with one question or a linked set and three rounds.

variants.name: Knowledge Café
variants.description: People share what they know on a topic, with no set output.

variants.name: Future Café
variants.description: The questions are about what the group wants in a few years' time.

variants.name: Solution Café
variants.description: Each table works on answers to a stated problem.

variants.name: Question Café
variants.description: Tables produce questions, not answers, to shape later work.

variants.name: Data Café
variants.description: Each table gets a set of data or findings to make sense of.

variants.name: Hybrid World Café
variants.description: Some tables are in the room and some are online breakout rooms.

mechanics: Dialogic learning; collective intelligence
cautions: You get themes, not decisions and not skills. Follow it with a step that decides or acts, and do not promise more than that.
theory: Dialogic learning; collective intelligence
howTo: Set out tables of four or five with paper tablecloths and pens. Write one clear, open question.
Round one, 20 minutes: each table discusses the question and writes or draws on the paper.
One host stays at each table. Everyone else moves to different tables.
The host sums up in a minute, then the new group builds on it. Run two or three rounds.
Each table calls out its main points and you group them on a wall.
Say what will happen to the output.
time: 60 to 90 minutes
group: 12 to 200 people, at tables of four or five

name: Open Space Technology
