description: An event with no fixed agenda. Participants propose the sessions they want to hold, everyone chooses where to go, and each session writes up what it found.
bestFor: Reach for it when the expertise is in the group, there is a shared question, and you cannot know in advance which topics matter.

variants.name: Full-day Open Space
variants.description: Three or four rounds of sessions, with time to bring the results together.

variants.name: Half-day Open Space
variants.description: Two rounds of sessions.

variants.name: Marketplace of skills
variants.description: People offer to teach something they know and others sign up.

variants.name: Unconference
variants.description: A conference where the people attending set the agenda on the day.

variants.name: Participant-led breakout exchange
variants.description: One slot inside a normal programme where participants propose the breakout topics.

variants.name: Open agenda with convergence
variants.description: It ends with a round that votes on priorities and names owners for actions.

mechanics: Self-determination; social learning; emergence
cautions: With a vague theme or no write-up, nothing lasts beyond the day. It is the wrong tool for content everyone must cover, because people choose what to attend.
theory: Self-determination; social learning; emergence
howTo: State a theme that people care about. Put a blank grid of times and spaces on the wall.
Sit everyone in a circle and explain the rules, including that anyone may leave a session where they are neither learning nor contributing.
Invite anyone to write a topic, announce it and pin it to a slot.
People sign up and the sessions run, 45 to 60 minutes each.
The person who called each session makes sure notes go on a shared wall or document.
Close in the circle with what people are taking away and any next steps.
time: Half a day to two days
group: 20 to several hundred people

name: Fishbowl discussion
description: A few people sit in an inner circle and hold a discussion. Everyone else sits around them and watches, with something specific to look for.
bestFor: Reach for it when you want to show a group what a good discussion looks like, or air different views without everyone talking at once.

variants.name: Closed fishbowl
variants.description: The inner circle stays the same throughout.

variants.name: Open fishbowl
variants.description: One inner chair is kept empty for anyone to come in and speak, and when they do, someone else leaves.

variants.name: Rotating fishbowl
variants.description: The inner group changes at set times.

variants.name: Leader fishbowl
variants.description: Senior leaders talk in the middle while staff listen, and then the two swap.

variants.name: Expert-practitioner fishbowl
variants.description: Experts and people who do the job discuss a topic together in the middle.

variants.name: Case fishbowl
variants.description: The inner circle works through a case and has to reach a decision.

variants.name: Decision fishbowl
variants.description: The inner circle makes a real decision in the open while the rest observe how.

mechanics: Observational learning; dialogic learning
cautions: Observers switch off without a task, and senior people in the middle can silence the rest. Give every observer something to look for and choose the inner circle with care.
theory: Observational learning; dialogic learning
howTo: Set four to six chairs in the middle and the rest around them.
Give the inner circle a question. Give the outer circle a task, such as noting the arguments used or how people listen.
Run the discussion for 15 to 20 minutes. Observers stay silent.
Ask observers what they noticed, then ask the inner circle how it felt.
Swap people in and repeat, or open it up to the whole group.
time: 30 to 45 minutes
group: Four to six in the middle, up to 30 watching

name: Reciprocal teaching
description: Small groups read a hard text in sections. For each section, members take turns to predict what comes next, ask a question, clear up confusing parts and sum it up.
bestFor: Reach for it when people must understand difficult written material, such as a policy, a research report or a technical specification.

variants.name: Predict-question-clarify-summarise
variants.description: The standard four roles, taken in that order.

variants.name: Rotating discussion roles
variants.description: The same idea of rotating roles, used for a discussion and not a text.

variants.name: Evidence-reading reciprocal teaching
variants.description: The text is a research paper or a data report.

variants.name: Policy-reading reciprocal teaching
variants.description: The text is a policy, contract or regulation.

tierRaw: A/B - Strong in literacy, conditional elsewhere
mechanics: Metacognition; scaffolding; social constructivism
cautions: It was designed for reading, so do not expect it to work unchanged for other skills. The roles can become a ritual, so listen in and push for real questions.
theory: Metacognition; scaffolding; social constructivism
howTo: Split the text into four or five sections.
Form groups of four and hand out role cards: predictor, questioner, clarifier, summariser.
Model one section yourself, playing all four roles aloud.
Groups read a section in silence, then each role speaks in turn for about a minute.
Rotate the roles for the next section.
Close with each group giving a one-sentence summary of the whole text.
time: 30 to 45 minutes
group: Groups of four

name: On-the-job training
description: People learn a task by doing it in the real job, with someone experienced beside them who shows the standard, watches and gives feedback.
bestFor: Reach for it when the task is best learnt on real work and people need to be productive quickly.

variants.name: Buddy-led on-the-job training
variants.description: A peer who does the job trains the newcomer.

variants.name: Supervisor-led on-the-job training
variants.description: The line manager does the training.

variants.name: Structured task sign-off
variants.description: A checklist of tasks, each signed off when the learner meets the standard.

variants.name: Guided first performance
variants.description: The first go at a real task is done with the trainer beside the learner.

variants.name: On-the-job training with growing responsibility
variants.description: The learner takes on harder tasks, or more of the job, by stages.

variants.name: On-the-job training in recovering from errors
variants.description: The learner practises what to do when things go wrong.

variants.name: On-the-job training across shifts
variants.description: The learner trains on different shifts to see how the work varies.

mechanics: Situated learning; near transfer; cognitive apprenticeship
cautions: Left informal, it turns into sitting next to someone and copying their shortcuts. Write the standards, pick and brief the trainers, and check each task before sign-off.
theory: Situated learning; near transfer; cognitive apprenticeship
howTo: List the tasks to learn and write the standard for each.
Choose a trainer who does the task well and brief them on how to coach.
The trainer shows the task, then the learner does it while the trainer watches.
Give feedback straight away, against the standard.
The learner repeats with less help each time.
Sign the task off only when the learner meets the standard unaided.
time: 30 to 60 minutes a task, repeated over days or weeks
group: One to one

name: Job instruction training
description: A four-step way to teach a task one to one: prepare the learner, show the task with its key points, have them do it while explaining, then check back later.
bestFor: Reach for it when a standard task must be done the same way every time.

variants.name: Four-step job instruction
variants.description: The full method as described above.

variants.name: Standard work demonstration
variants.description: The trainer shows the agreed standard way of doing the task, working from the written standard.

variants.name: Key-point coaching
variants.description: A short refresher on the key points only, for someone who already knows the steps.

variants.name: Job breakdown sheet practice
variants.description: Trainers practise writing breakdown sheets for their own tasks.

mechanics: Behavioural task analysis; modelling; guided practice
cautions: It teaches one fixed way, which suits standard tasks and does not suit judgement calls. For work that changes case by case, add scenarios or coaching.
theory: Behavioural task analysis; modelling; guided practice
howTo: Before you start, write a breakdown sheet: each main step, its key points and the reason for each.
Prepare: put the learner at ease and find out what they already know.
Present: do the task three times. Say the steps, then add the key points, then add the reasons.
Try out: the learner does it, first in silence while you correct, then while saying the steps, key points and reasons.
Follow up: let them work alone, tell them who to ask, and check often at first and then less.
time: 20 to 45 minutes a task
group: One to one, or one trainer with two or three learners

name: Apprenticeship
description: A long work-based programme. A beginner does real work under an experienced person, takes on harder tasks over months or years and usually studies alongside.
bestFor: Reach for it when the craft takes years to build and you are bringing new people into an occupation.

variants.name: Traditional craft apprenticeship
variants.description: A skilled trade learnt beside a master of it.

variants.name: Digital apprenticeship
variants.description: An apprenticeship in a technology role, such as software or data.

variants.name: Rotational apprenticeship
variants.description: The apprentice moves through several teams.

variants.name: Degree apprenticeship
variants.description: Paid work combined with part-time study for a university degree.

variants.name: Internal talent apprenticeship
variants.description: Existing staff retrain into a new role.

variants.name: Project apprenticeship
variants.description: The learning is organised around a series of real projects.

variants.name: Cognitive apprenticeship pathway
variants.description: A long version of cognitive apprenticeship, where the supervisor explains their thinking throughout.

mechanics: Situated learning; legitimate peripheral participation; cognitive apprenticeship
cautions: Quality depends on the supervisor and on the range of work the apprentice gets to see. Train the supervisors, and rotate apprentices so they do not learn one narrow way.
theory: Situated learning; legitimate peripheral participation; cognitive apprenticeship
howTo: Map the skills of the role and put them in order from simple to complex.
Give each apprentice a named supervisor who has time set aside.
Start with real but low-risk tasks, and add harder ones as each is signed off.
Add learning away from the job, such as a day a week of study.
Review progress every month against the skills map.
End with an assessment of real work.
time: One to four years
group: One supervisor with one to three apprentices

name: Job rotation
description: People move through several roles, teams or sites for a set time each, to see how the whole organisation fits together.
bestFor: Reach for it with future leaders and others who need to understand how other teams work.

variants.name: Functional rotation
variants.description: The moves are between departments, such as sales, product and support.

variants.name: Market rotation
variants.description: The moves are between the countries or regions the organisation sells in.

variants.name: Client rotation
variants.description: The moves are between client accounts.

variants.name: Short micro-rotation
variants.description: A few days to two weeks in another team.

variants.name: Shadow rotation
variants.description: The person observes in each team and does not do the work.

variants.name: Leadership rotation
variants.description: The person takes management roles in different areas.

variants.name: International rotation
variants.description: The person works in another country for a period.

variants.name: Project-based rotation
variants.description: The person moves between projects, not departments.

mechanics: Experiential learning; boundary crossing; job enrichment
cautions: Without goals and real work it becomes a tour, and people leave each team just as they become useful. Set goals for every placement and build in time to reflect.
theory: Experiential learning; boundary crossing; job enrichment
howTo: Set learning goals for each placement: what to understand and what to be able to do.
Agree a real piece of work in each team, not just watching.
Name a host in each team who briefs, supports and reviews.
Give each placement enough time to contribute, often four to twelve weeks.
After each one, the learner writes what they learnt and talks it over with a coach or manager.
End with a review of how the parts connect.
time: Three to eighteen months in total
group: Individuals, often run as a small cohort

name: Stretch assignment
description: A person is given real work a step beyond what they can comfortably do, with a manager or mentor to support them and a review at the end.
bestFor: Reach for it when a capable person is ready to grow into leadership or to handle unfamiliar situations.

variants.name: Acting-up assignment
variants.description: The person covers a more senior role for a time.

variants.name: High-visibility project
variants.description: The person leads work that senior people are watching.

variants.name: Turnaround assignment
variants.description: The person takes on something that is failing.

variants.name: New-market assignment
variants.description: The person works in a market or sector that is new to them or to the organisation.

variants.name: Cross-functional stretch
variants.description: The person leads work across departments they do not control.

variants.name: Client-facing stretch
variants.description: The person takes on direct responsibility for a client.

variants.name: Innovation stretch
variants.description: The person builds something new with no set path.

variants.name: Crisis-response stretch
variants.description: The person takes a role in handling a crisis, with close support.

mechanics: Experiential learning; challenge–support; self-efficacy
cautions: Without support it turns into overload, or extra work with no reward. Take something off their plate, agree the support at the start and offer these chances fairly.
theory: Experiential learning; challenge–support; self-efficacy
howTo: Choose an assignment that is new in one or two ways, such as scale or audience, not in every way.
Agree what they should learn from it, as well as what they should deliver.
Name the support: who they can ask, and what happens if it starts going wrong.
Hold check-ins every week or two to talk about what is hard.
Review at the end: what they did, what they learnt and what comes next.
Recognise the extra work, in workload or in pay.
time: Three to twelve months
group: One person, with a manager or mentor

name: Learning in the flow of work
description: Help that reaches people while they do the real task, inside or next to the tool they use: a prompt, a short guide, a person to ask. Nobody leaves work to attend a course.
bestFor: Use it when a tool or process changes often and people need the answer at the moment they are doing the task.

variants.name: Embedded workflow prompt
variants.description: A short reminder appears inside the tool at the step where people usually go wrong.

variants.name: Contextual job aid
variants.description: A one-page guide is linked from the exact screen, form or template it applies to.

variants.name: In-app walkthrough
variants.description: The software itself leads the user through a task step by step, on their own real data.

variants.name: Searchable knowledge assistant
variants.description: People type a question into a search box or chat tool and get the answer from your own approved guidance.

variants.name: Moment-of-need micro-lesson
variants.description: A lesson of two or three minutes is linked from the task, for people doing it for the first time.

variants.name: AI workflow copilot
variants.description: An AI assistant approved by the organisation suggests the next step or a draft as people work, and the person checks it before using it.

variants.name: Manager-triggered learning nudge
variants.description: The manager sends the prompt or resource just before a team member takes on the task.

variants.name: Task-linked expert office hour
variants.description: An expert holds a regular open slot, for example 30 minutes a week, where people bring the task they are stuck on.

tierRaw: D/B - Practitioner framework with supported mechanisms
mechanics: Performance support; situated cognition; transfer of training
cautions: People can learn to click through the steps without understanding the reason for them. Pair the help with a short explanation or practice session whenever judgement matters.
theory: Performance support; situated cognition; transfer of training
howTo: Pick one task people get stuck on. Watch two or three people do it and note the exact point where they stop.
Write the smallest help that gets them past that point: a prompt, a one-page guide or a two-minute clip.
Put it where the work happens: in the tool, pinned in the team channel or linked from the ticket template.
Tell people it exists and show it once in a team meeting, on a real task.
After two weeks, ask five users whether they used it and what was missing. Fix it or remove it.
Add a short session on the idea behind the task if people follow the steps but cannot explain why.
time: Half a day to build one piece of help. Each use takes 1 to 5 minutes.
group: Individuals at work, any number

name: Job aids and in-tool guidance
description: Checklists, decision trees and step-by-step guides that people follow while doing a task. The aid holds the detail so that nobody has to hold it in their head.
bestFor: Use it for tasks people do rarely, new systems, and steps where a slip is costly.

variants.name: Checklist
variants.description: A short list of steps or checks that people tick off in order.

variants.name: Decision tree
variants.description: A diagram of yes or no questions that leads to the right action for the situation.

variants.name: Interactive troubleshooting guide
variants.description: An on-screen guide asks what the user sees and shows the next thing to try.

variants.name: In-product coach marks
variants.description: Small pop-up labels inside the software point at a button or field and say what it is for.

variants.name: Context card
variants.description: A pocket-sized card sits at the desk, machine or meeting room where the task happens.

variants.name: Smart form with guidance
variants.description: The form explains each field as you fill it in and warns you when an entry looks wrong.

variants.name: QR-linked field guide
variants.description: A QR code on the equipment or wall opens the guide for that exact item on a phone.

variants.name: Augmented overlay instruction
variants.description: Instructions appear on a phone, tablet or headset view, laid over the real equipment.

mechanics: Distributed cognition; cognitive offloading; performance support
cautions: People can lean on the aid and never learn the task, which is fine for rare tasks. Where speed or memory matters, take the aid away in practice once people are accurate.
theory: Distributed cognition; cognitive offloading; performance support
howTo: Choose a task that is done rarely or goes wrong often. Ask an experienced person to talk you through it while you write down each step.
Pick the format. Use a checklist for fixed steps, a decision tree for 'it depends' tasks and a walkthrough for software.
Draft it on one page. Start each step with a verb and use the words that appear on the screen or the kit.
Give the draft to someone new and watch them use it without help. Every place they hesitate is an edit.
Put the aid where the task happens and name one owner who updates it when the task changes.
If people must do the task from memory, practise in the session with the aid first, then without it.
time: 1 to 3 hours to draft and test one aid
group: Individuals at work. Test with 2 or 3 users first.

name: Shadowing
description: A learner spends time beside an experienced colleague doing real work, watches how they handle it, and then asks why they did what they did.
bestFor: Use it for work that is hard to write down, such as handling clients and stakeholders, and for people settling into a new role.

variants.name: Job shadowing
variants.description: The learner follows one person through a normal working day or half day.

variants.name: Reverse shadowing
variants.description: The experienced person watches the learner work and comments afterwards.

variants.name: Executive shadowing
variants.description: The learner follows a senior leader through meetings to see how decisions get made.

variants.name: Customer shadowing
variants.description: The learner watches a customer use the product or service in the customer's own setting.

variants.name: Field ride-along
variants.description: The learner travels with a field worker, such as a sales rep or engineer, for a day of visits.

variants.name: Meeting shadow
variants.description: The learner sits in on one meeting or call and debriefs it with the host afterwards.

variants.name: Role safari
variants.description: The learner spends a short time with several different roles in turn to see how the work connects.

variants.name: Shadow-and-debrief
variants.description: Each short stretch of watching is followed at once by a set debrief, repeated several times in a day.

mechanics: Observational learning; situated cognition
cautions: Watching alone teaches little. Without set questions and a debrief the learner sees what happened and misses why, so always add the debrief and a chance to try it.
theory: Observational learning; situated cognition
howTo: Agree the purpose with both people. Give the learner three things to look for, for example how the colleague opens a difficult call.
Brief the host. Ask them to say their thinking out loud where they can, and to flag anything confidential beforehand.
The learner watches for 1 to 3 hours and notes what the host did and what seemed to prompt it. They do not join in unless invited.
Debrief for 20 minutes straight afterwards. The learner asks 'What were you noticing when you did that?' about two or three moments.
The learner picks one thing to try in their own work that week.
Follow up with a turn where the learner does the task and the host watches.
time: 1 to 3 hours of watching, plus a 20-minute debrief
group: One learner with one host

name: After-action review
description: A short team conversation straight after a piece of work. The team compares what it meant to happen with what did happen, works out why, and agrees what to do differently next time.
bestFor: Use it after a project, a live event, a client engagement or a practice exercise, while memories are fresh.

variants.name: Four-question AAR
variants.description: The standard version, built on the four questions about intent, outcome, causes and changes.

variants.name: Hot debrief
variants.description: A 10-minute version held within minutes of finishing, standing up, to catch first impressions.

variants.name: Cold debrief
variants.description: A longer review held days later, once data is in and feelings have settled.

variants.name: Video-assisted AAR
variants.description: The team watches a recording of key moments before discussing them, so the review rests on what can be seen.

variants.name: Cross-team AAR
variants.description: Two or more teams that worked on the same thing review it together, with a facilitator from outside both.

variants.name: Simulation AAR
variants.description: The review follows a practice exercise or simulation, so mistakes carry no real cost.

variants.name: Client-engagement AAR
variants.description: The team reviews a piece of client work, and may invite the client for part of it.

variants.name: Data-backed AAR
variants.description: The review starts from numbers, logs or timelines gathered beforehand, not from memory.

mechanics: Reflective practice; experiential learning; team learning
cautions: It turns into blame, or into a ritual that changes nothing. Have the leader name one of their own mistakes first, work from facts, and check last time's actions at the start.
theory: Reflective practice; experiential learning; team learning
howTo: Set the rule at the start: 'We are here to learn, not to find who is at fault.' Bring any facts you have, such as timings, numbers or the plan.
Ask 'What did we mean to happen?' Write the answer where everyone can see it. Allow 5 minutes.
Ask 'What actually happened?' Go round the group so the quieter people speak before the most senior person. Allow 10 minutes.
Ask 'Why was there a difference?' Keep asking about causes in the work, not about who did it. Allow 10 minutes.
Ask 'What will we keep, and what will we change next time?' Limit it to two or three actions, each with a name against it.
Send the actions round the same day and open the next review by checking them.
time: 20 to 45 minutes
group: The team that did the work, ideally 4 to 12 people

name: Learning retrospective
description: A regular team meeting, often every two to four weeks, where the team looks back at how it worked, picks what to change, and agrees one small thing to try before the next one.
bestFor: Use it with teams that work in repeating cycles and have the authority to change how they work.

variants.name: Start-stop-continue
variants.description: Notes are sorted under three headings: what to start doing, stop doing and continue doing.

variants.name: Sailboat retrospective
variants.description: The team draws a boat and adds notes for wind (what pushes it on), anchors (what holds it back) and rocks (risks ahead).

variants.name: Timeline retrospective
variants.description: The team draws the period as a timeline and marks the high and low points before discussing them.

variants.name: Learning delta review
variants.description: Each person states one thing they now know or can do that they could not at the last review, and one gap that remains.

variants.name: Experiment retrospective
variants.description: The meeting reviews only the experiments agreed last time and decides whether to keep, change or drop each one.

mechanics: Double-loop learning; reflexivity; continuous improvement
cautions: It dies when the same complaints come up each time and nothing changes. Keep actions small and inside the team's control, and send the rest upwards.
theory: Double-loop learning; reflexivity; continuous improvement
howTo: Book 45 to 60 minutes at the end of each cycle. Open by checking what happened to last time's actions.
Give everyone 5 minutes to write sticky notes in silence under three headings, such as start, stop and continue.
Group similar notes together. Give each person three dots to vote for what matters most.
Discuss the top one or two items for 15 minutes each. Ask 'What is in our power to change here?'
Agree one or two small experiments with an owner and a way to tell whether each one worked.
Pass anything the team cannot change to the person who can, by name.
time: 45 to 60 minutes, every 2 to 4 weeks
group: One team of 4 to 10

name: Retrieval practice
description: People pull what they have learned out of memory, with notes closed, by answering questions, writing down all they recall or working a case. They then check their answer.
bestFor: Use it for anything people must remember and use later without looking it up.

variants.name: Free recall
variants.description: People write down all they can remember about a topic with no prompts.

variants.name: Cued recall
variants.description: People answer from a hint, such as a keyword, a diagram with blank labels or the first step.

variants.name: Practice quiz
variants.description: A short set of questions is answered without notes and marked by the learner.

variants.name: Brain dump
variants.description: Everyone has two minutes to write all they remember on a blank page, then compares with a neighbour.

variants.name: Two-stage quiz
variants.description: People answer alone first, then answer the same questions again in a small group and agree one answer.

variants.name: Scenario retrieval
variants.description: The question is a short work situation, and people recall what to do in it.

variants.name: Application retrieval
variants.description: People recall a principle and then apply it to a new example they have not seen before.

variants.name: Peer questioning
variants.description: Learners write questions for each other and take turns asking and answering.

variants.name: Cumulative quiz
variants.description: Each quiz includes questions from all earlier sessions, not only the latest one.

variants.name: Confidence-rated retrieval
variants.description: People rate how sure they are of each answer before seeing the right one, to show up confident errors.

mechanics: Testing effect; retrieval-strength theory
cautions: It goes wrong when it feels like a test or asks for trivia. Keep it unmarked, always give the answers, and ask about things people will use.
theory: Testing effect; retrieval-strength theory
howTo: Choose three to five things from earlier in the session, or from last time, that people need on the job.
Write questions that ask people to use the idea, for example 'A client says X. What do you check first?'
Ask everyone to close their notes and answer alone, in writing, for 3 to 5 minutes. No marks are recorded.
Have pairs compare answers for 2 minutes. Then give the correct answers and say why.
Ask people to mark what they missed. Bring those points back in the next round.
Tell the group why you are doing it: recalling helps memory more than rereading does, and it feels harder.
time: 5 to 10 minutes, several times across a programme
group: Individuals first, then pairs. Any group size.

name: Spaced practice
description: Practice on the same material is spread over several short sessions with gaps between them. The alternative, one long block on one day, is what this replaces.
bestFor: Use it when people need to remember something weeks or months after the training.

variants.name: Expanding intervals
variants.description: Each gap is longer than the last, for example one day, then three days, then two weeks.

variants.name: Equal intervals
variants.description: The gaps stay the same length, for example once a week for six weeks.

variants.name: End-of-day booster
variants.description: The last ten minutes of the day are a recall exercise on that day's key points.

variants.name: Two-day booster
variants.description: A short quiz or task arrives two days after the session.

variants.name: Weekly booster
variants.description: One short practice task arrives each week, often in a team meeting.

variants.name: Monthly booster
variants.description: A longer review of 20 to 30 minutes is held once a month to keep older material alive.

variants.name: Spaced scenario sequence
variants.description: A series of short work situations is released over several weeks, each a little harder than the last.

variants.name: Spaced peer challenge
variants.description: Pairs set each other a question or task at agreed intervals after the course.

mechanics: Spacing effect; consolidation; desirable difficulties
cautions: Sending the slides again is not practice. Each visit must ask people to recall or do something, and the gaps should suit how long the learning has to last.
theory: Spacing effect; consolidation; desirable difficulties
howTo: List the five to ten things that must last beyond the course.
Plan at least three return visits, for example the end of the day, two days later and two weeks later.
Make each visit a task, not a reminder. Use questions answered from memory or a short case to work through, for 5 to 10 minutes.
Put the visits in calendars before the course ends, or build them into team meetings.
Mix earlier topics into each visit so that nothing is seen only once.
Lengthen the gaps if people need to remember for longer. There is no single correct interval.
time: 5 to 10 minutes per visit, 3 to 5 visits over several weeks
group: Individuals or the whole group

name: Successive relearning
description: People test themselves on the same material in several sessions spread over days or weeks. In each session they keep going until they get every item right once.
bestFor: Use it for a small set of knowledge that people must recall quickly and correctly, such as safety rules, product facts or key terms.

variants.name: Criterion-based relearning
variants.description: You set a target, such as every item correct once per session, and people stop when they reach it.

variants.name: Spaced flashcard mastery
variants.description: The routine is run with a deck of flashcards, and a card leaves the pile only when answered correctly.

variants.name: Spaced scenario mastery
variants.description: The items are short work situations, and people repeat each one until they choose the right action.

variants.name: Cumulative oral retrieval
variants.description: Pairs quiz each other out loud, and each session includes items from all the earlier ones.

mechanics: Retrieval practice plus spacing
cautions: It takes real time, so it suits a short list of must-know items. It will not build judgement or a complex skill on its own.
theory: Retrieval practice plus spacing
howTo: Choose a small set: 15 to 30 items that people must know without looking them up.
Turn each one into a question with a clear right answer. Use cards or a quiz tool.
In session one, people answer from memory and check. Wrong items go back in the pile until each has been answered correctly once.
Repeat the same routine two or three more times, with a few days between sessions.
Expect each session to be shorter than the last. Tell people this at the start so they can see progress.
Follow with practice that uses the knowledge in a realistic task.
time: 10 to 20 minutes per session, 3 or 4 sessions over 2 to 3 weeks
group: Individuals, or pairs testing each other

name: Interleaved practice
description: Practice tasks of different but related types are mixed together in one set. For each task people first have to work out which approach fits, then use it.
bestFor: Use it once people know the basics and need to tell similar situations apart.

variants.name: Mixed problem types
variants.description: A practice set shuffles several kinds of problem so the type is not given away by its position.

variants.name: Mixed client scenarios
variants.description: Short client situations of different kinds are presented in random order for people to diagnose and respond to.

variants.name: Mixed skill stations
variants.description: Small groups rotate round tables, each with a different skill to practise for 10 minutes.

variants.name: Randomised case ordering
variants.description: The same set of cases is given to each person or group in a different shuffled order.

variants.name: Interleaved technical drills
variants.description: Short hands-on drills for different procedures are alternated in one practice block.

variants.name: Interleaved judgement practice
variants.description: People judge a mixed run of examples, such as good, borderline and poor work, and explain each call.

mechanics: Discrimination learning; contextual interference
cautions: Mixing too early confuses beginners, and mixing unrelated topics adds effort without benefit. Teach each type on its own first and mix only things people could confuse.
theory: Discrimination learning; contextual interference
howTo: Teach each type separately first, with a few practice tasks of that type only.
Build a mixed set of 8 to 12 tasks that covers three or four related types in shuffled order, with no labels.
Ask people to write down which type each task is, and why, before they solve it.
Review in pairs and then as a group. Spend most of the time on how they told the types apart.
Warn people that mixed practice feels harder and slower than practising one type at a time.
Keep mixing in later sessions, adding each new type to the set.
time: 20 to 40 minutes
group: Individuals or pairs, any group size

name: Microlearning
description: A very short piece of learning, usually two to five minutes, that covers one idea or one action and can be used on its own.
bestFor: Use it for refreshers after a course, for help at the moment of need, and for spaced follow-up.

variants.name: Single-concept micro-lesson
variants.description: One idea is explained with one example in a few minutes.

variants.name: Micro-video
variants.description: A clip of one to three minutes shows one thing being done.

variants.name: Micro-podcast
variants.description: A short audio piece of three to five minutes tells one story or makes one point.

variants.name: Micro-scenario
variants.description: A short work situation asks for one decision and shows what follows from it.

variants.name: Micro-quiz
variants.description: Two or three questions are answered from memory, with the answers shown straight after.

variants.name: Micro-coaching prompt
variants.description: A single question arrives for the person to think about before or after a task, such as 'What will you ask first?'

variants.name: Micro-demonstration
variants.description: An expert shows one step and says what they are paying attention to as they do it.

variants.name: Micro-challenge
variants.description: A small task is set to do in real work today, with something to show for it.

variants.name: Daily learning card
variants.description: One card a day arrives with a tip, a question or an example.

variants.name: Chat-based microlearning
variants.description: Short lessons and questions arrive as messages in the chat tool the team already uses.

mechanics: Cognitive load management; spacing; just-in-time learning
cautions: Short does not mean effective. A pile of unconnected pieces leaves people with fragments, so link each one to a larger course or map and include something to do.
theory: Cognitive load management; spacing; just-in-time learning
howTo: Write one sentence saying what the person will be able to do afterwards. If it needs 'and', split it into two pieces.
Choose the format to suit the action: a clip to show how, a card to remind, a question to practise.
Cut all that does not serve that one action. Aim for two to five minutes.
End with something to do: a question to answer or a step to try on the next real task.
Show where the piece sits in the bigger picture, with a line or a link to what comes before and after.
Check whether people used it by asking a few of them, not only by counting views.
time: 2 to 5 minutes per piece
group: Individuals, any number

name: Nudges and reminders
description: Short messages that arrive at the moment they are useful. Each one reminds a person to try something, recall something or plan when they will do it.
bestFor: Use them after training to prompt people to apply one specific thing in their real work.

variants.name: Calendar nudge
variants.description: A short calendar entry is placed at the time the action should happen.

variants.name: Teams or Slack nudge
variants.description: The message is posted in the team's chat channel or sent as a direct message.

variants.name: Manager nudge
variants.description: The manager gets a prompt to ask their team member about the new skill.

variants.name: Social proof nudge
variants.description: The message shares a true example of what colleagues have already tried.

variants.name: Implementation-intention prompt
variants.description: The message asks the person to complete the sentence 'When X happens, I will do Y.'

variants.name: Pre-task cue
variants.description: The reminder arrives just before a known task, such as a client call.

variants.name: Post-task reflection cue
variants.description: The message arrives after the task and asks what went well and what to change.

variants.name: Deadline-linked nudge
variants.description: The prompt is tied to a real deadline, such as the day before a report is due.

mechanics: Nudge theory; implementation intentions; cue-dependent behaviour
cautions: A reminder cannot make up for missing time, tools or support from a manager. Too many messages get ignored, so send few, make each specific and stop after a few weeks.
theory: Nudge theory; implementation intentions; cue-dependent behaviour
howTo: Pick one behaviour from the training and the moment it should happen, for example before the weekly one-to-one.
Write the message in under 40 words. Name the action and the moment: 'Before your one-to-one today, write the one question you will open with.'
Send it through a channel people already check, timed just before that moment.
Plan three to five messages over four weeks, each a little different. Then stop.
Include one that asks people to reply with what they tried, so you learn what is happening.
Check with managers that people have the time and tools to act on the message.
time: A minute to read. About an hour to write and schedule a set.
group: Individuals, any number

name: Flashcards and quiz cards
description: Cards with a question or prompt on one side and the answer on the other. People answer from memory, turn the card to check, and repeat the ones they missed.
bestFor: Use them for terms, facts, warning signs and simple rules that people need to recall quickly.

variants.name: Leitner box
variants.description: Cards move forward through numbered boxes when answered correctly and back to box one when missed, and later boxes are reviewed less often.

variants.name: Digital adaptive flashcards
variants.description: An app shows the cards you get wrong more often and the ones you know less often.

variants.name: Scenario flashcards
variants.description: The front of the card describes a short work situation and the back gives the right action.

variants.name: Visual cue cards
variants.description: The front shows a picture, screenshot or diagram, and people say what it shows or what to do.

variants.name: Team quiz cards
variants.description: Small teams draw cards in turn and answer together, with or without scoring.

mechanics: Retrieval practice; spacing; feedback
cautions: Cards build recall of facts, not the skill of using them. Follow them with practice on realistic tasks, and stop people turning the card before they have answered.
theory: Retrieval practice; spacing; feedback
howTo: Write 15 to 30 cards with one question and one short answer each. Ask 'What do you do when...' as well as 'What is...'
Show people how to use them: say or write the answer before turning the card over.
Sort the cards into two piles, right and wrong. Go through the wrong pile again until it is empty.
Come back to the full deck after a day, then after a few days, then after a week.
In a session, have pairs quiz each other for 5 to 10 minutes.
Follow the cards with a task that uses the knowledge in a realistic situation.
time: 5 to 10 minutes per round
group: Individuals or pairs

name: Learning journal
description: A private notebook where people write, at set points, what they tried, what happened, what they still do not understand, and what they will try next.
bestFor: Use it on programmes that run over weeks, to help people notice their own progress and plan their next step.

variants.name: Structured journal
variants.description: Every entry answers the same fixed prompts.

variants.name: Critical incident journal
variants.description: Each entry describes one event that mattered and what the writer takes from it.

variants.name: Decision journal
variants.description: The writer records a decision, the reasons and the result they expect, then checks later what happened.

variants.name: Audio journal
variants.description: Entries are spoken into a phone as voice notes.

variants.name: Photo journal
variants.description: Each entry is a photo of work or a moment, with a line saying why it matters.

variants.name: Learning-log evidence journal
variants.description: Entries record dated evidence of practice, such as what was done and who saw it, for use in an assessment or portfolio.

mechanics: Metacognition; reflective practice; self-regulated learning
cautions: Without prompts, entries turn into vague summaries or what people think the trainer wants to hear. Use specific prompts, keep it private and never mark it.
theory: Metacognition; reflective practice; self-regulated learning
howTo: Give everyone a notebook or a template with three or four fixed prompts.
Use prompts that ask for specifics: 'What did I try? What happened? What will I do differently? What question do I still have?'
Protect 5 to 10 quiet minutes for writing at the end of each session. Do not leave it as homework only.
Say clearly that the journal is private. Nobody has to show it or read from it.
Invite people to share one line with a partner if they wish.
At the midpoint and the end, ask people to read back through their entries and write what has changed.
time: 5 to 10 minutes per entry
group: Individuals, any group size

name: Self-paced e-learning
description: An online course that people work through alone, in their own time. It usually combines short explanations, examples, questions and practice tasks.
bestFor: Use it for basic knowledge that many people need, for required compliance topics, and to prepare people for a live session.

variants.name: Linear module
variants.description: Everyone goes through the same screens in the same order.

variants.name: Explorable module
variants.description: People choose which sections to open and in what order from a menu.

variants.name: Scenario-led module
variants.description: The module opens with a work situation, and the content is taught through the decisions it calls for.

variants.name: Adaptive module
variants.description: The module skips what a person already knows and adds help where they get questions wrong.

variants.name: Resource-first module
variants.description: People are given a task and a library of resources, and look up what they need to complete it.

variants.name: Video-led module
variants.description: Short videos carry the explanation, with questions between them.

variants.name: Interactive workbook
variants.description: A digital document that people type into, with exercises and space for notes.

variants.name: Cohort-paced asynchronous module
variants.description: A group works through the same module in the same week and discusses it in a forum or chat, each at times that suit them.

mechanics: Multimedia learning; self-regulated learning
cautions: A completed course does not show that someone can do the job, and many people click through while doing other things. Keep modules short, build in questions that need thought, and check the skill another way.
theory: Multimedia learning; self-regulated learning
howTo: Write down what people must be able to do at the end. Build the practice questions and tasks first.
Split the content into sections of 5 to 10 minutes, each with one aim.
After each explanation add a question or task that makes people use it, with feedback on their answer.
State the total time at the start and let people stop and return where they left off.
Test it with two or three real learners. Watch where they skip, guess or get lost.
Add a human touchpoint, such as a manager conversation or a live follow-up session.
time: 20 to 40 minutes per module, in sections of 5 to 10 minutes
group: Individuals, any number

name: Flipped learning
description: People take in the explanation before the session, by video, reading or audio. The live time is then spent on practice, problems and feedback.
bestFor: Use it when live time is short or expensive and you want it spent on practice.

variants.name: Video-first flip
variants.description: The pre-work is a short video explanation.

variants.name: Case-first flip
variants.description: People read a case beforehand and arrive ready to argue for a decision.

variants.name: Problem-first flip
variants.description: People attempt a problem before the session, and the live time starts from where they got stuck.

variants.name: Podcast-first flip
variants.description: The pre-work is an audio episode people can listen to while travelling.

variants.name: Data-first flip
variants.description: People look at a data set or report beforehand and bring one observation.

variants.name: Peer-teaching flip
variants.description: Each person prepares a different part beforehand and teaches it to the others in the session.

variants.name: AI-tutor flip
variants.description: People work through the material beforehand with an AI tutor that is limited to the course sources, and bring the questions it could not settle.

mechanics: Cognitive load; active learning; retrieval; social learning
cautions: It fails when the pre-work is long or when you repeat it in the room. People soon learn they need not do it, so keep it short and build the opening on it.
theory: Cognitive load; active learning; retrieval; social learning
howTo: Decide what people can take in alone and what needs the group. Send only the first kind beforehand.
Keep the pre-work to 20 minutes or less. Tell people how long it takes and why it matters.
Add a small task to the pre-work, such as three questions or one example to bring.
Open the live session with a five-minute quiz or task that relies on the pre-work. Do not present it again.
Spend the rest of the session on practice and feedback.
Have a ten-minute catch-up sheet ready for anyone who did not prepare, to do in the first break.
time: 15 to 20 minutes of preparation, plus the live session
group: Individuals beforehand, then the whole group

name: Virtual instructor-led training
description: A live session on a video platform such as Zoom or Teams. A trainer teaches people in different places at the same time, using chat, polls, breakout rooms and shared documents.
bestFor: Use it when people are spread across sites or countries and still need live discussion, demonstration or coaching.

variants.name: Interactive webinar
variants.description: A larger audience mostly listens and takes part through polls, chat and questions.

variants.name: Virtual workshop
variants.description: A small group spends most of the time working on tasks in breakout rooms and shared documents.

variants.name: Virtual lab
variants.description: Each person practises hands-on in a practice copy of the software while the trainer watches and helps.

variants.name: Virtual studio
variants.description: People make something during the session and show it to the group for comment.

variants.name: Virtual simulation
variants.description: The group plays through a realistic situation online, in assigned roles, and debriefs it.

variants.name: Virtual coaching clinic
variants.description: People bring a real problem and are coached on it in turn while the others watch and learn.

variants.name: Virtual fishbowl
variants.description: A few people discuss with cameras on while the rest watch with cameras off, then swap.

variants.name: Virtual cohort seminar
variants.description: The same small group meets regularly online to discuss reading or cases.

mechanics: Community of inquiry; social presence; cognitive load
cautions: Long stretches of listening on screen lose people fast, and the informal chat of a real room does not happen by itself. Keep it short and active, and plan the moments where people talk to each other.
theory: Community of inquiry; social presence; cognitive load
howTo: Plan 60 to 90 minutes, with a five-minute break if you go past an hour.
Change what people are doing every 5 to 10 minutes: a poll, a chat question, a breakout, a shared document.
Get everyone to do something in the first three minutes, such as typing an answer in the chat.
Use breakout rooms of three or four for practice, with the task written in a shared document and a clear end time.
Have a second person manage the chat and the technology if the group is larger than 12.
Close with one written commitment from each person in the chat.
time: 60 to 90 minutes
group: 8 to 16 for a workshop. Breakouts of 3 or 4.

name: Blended learning
description: One programme that combines several formats, such as online modules, live sessions, practice at work and coaching, each chosen for what it does best and arranged in a planned order.
bestFor: Use it for programmes that run over weeks or months, especially when people are in different places.

variants.name: Online-before-live blend
variants.description: People study online first, then meet to practise.

variants.name: Live-before-online blend
variants.description: People meet first to get started and build trust, then continue online.

variants.name: Retreat-centred blend
variants.description: A residential retreat sits in the middle, with online preparation before and follow-up after.

variants.name: Hub-and-spoke blend
variants.description: One central live event is surrounded by smaller activities that people choose from.

variants.name: Global virtual plus local pod
variants.description: Everyone joins the same online sessions and then meets in person in small local groups to practise.

variants.name: Self-paced plus coaching
variants.description: People study alone and meet a coach at set points to apply it to their own work.

variants.name: Simulation plus workplace application
variants.description: People practise in a simulation first, then carry out the same task for real with support.

mechanics: Modality fit; spacing; transfer; community of inquiry
cautions: A set of formats placed side by side is not a blend. If the parts do not refer to each other, people skip the ones that feel optional.
theory: Modality fit; spacing; transfer; community of inquiry
howTo: List what people need to be able to do. Sort each item by what it needs: explanation, practice with feedback, or use at work.
Match the format to the need. Explanation can go online, practice with feedback goes live, and use happens at work with a manager or coach.
Put the parts in order so that each one uses the one before. Open each live session with a task that builds on the online part.
Draw the whole programme on one page with dates and time needed, and give it to learners and their managers.
Add a check between parts, such as a quiz or a short task, so you know who is ready for the next one.
After the first run, cut any part that people could skip without noticing.
time: Usually 4 to 12 weeks in total
group: A cohort of 8 to 16, working alone and together at different points

name: Mobile learning
description: Learning designed to be used on a phone, in short bursts, wherever the person is. It covers short lessons, checklists, quizzes and tasks that use the camera or microphone.
bestFor: Use it for people who are rarely at a desk, for refreshers, and for help on the spot.

variants.name: Mobile lesson
variants.description: A short lesson laid out as a few swipeable screens.

variants.name: Field checklist
variants.description: A checklist that is ticked off on the phone at the place of work.

variants.name: Photo evidence task
variants.description: The learner photographs their finished work and sends it for feedback.

variants.name: Location-based prompt
variants.description: A message or task appears when the person arrives at a set place.

variants.name: Mobile flashcard
variants.description: Question and answer cards to swipe through in spare minutes.

variants.name: Voice-note reflection
variants.description: The learner records a one-minute spoken note on what they tried and what happened.

variants.name: Mobile scenario
variants.description: A short work situation with choices to tap and a result for each.

variants.name: QR learning trail
variants.description: QR codes placed around a site each open a short piece of learning about that spot.

mechanics: Ubiquitous learning; spacing; situated learning
cautions: Small screens, interruptions and poor signal make phones a bad place for long or complicated material. Keep pieces short and check they work for people who use screen readers or larger text.
theory: Ubiquitous learning; spacing; situated learning
howTo: Find out when and where people will use it, such as on a shop floor or between visits.
Design for one hand and two minutes: one idea per screen, large text, few taps.
Use what the phone does well. Ask for a photo of the work, a voice note or a ticked checklist.
Make it work with a poor signal where you can, and add captions to any audio or video.
Test it on an old, small phone, outdoors.
Keep anything long or detailed for a session or a larger screen.
time: 1 to 5 minutes per use
group: Individuals, any number

name: Podcast / audio learning
description: Audio episodes that people listen to while commuting, walking or doing routine tasks. Episodes carry stories, interviews or short explanations.
bestFor: Use it to introduce a topic, share real stories or keep a group in touch between sessions.

variants.name: Expert interview podcast
variants.description: A host asks an experienced person how they handle real situations.

variants.name: Narrative case podcast
variants.description: One real case is told as a story, pausing at the decision points.

variants.name: Learner reflection podcast
variants.description: Learners record what they tried and learned, for the rest of the group to hear.

variants.name: Audio briefing
variants.description: A short spoken update on what is coming up and what to prepare.

variants.name: Guided reflection audio
variants.description: A voice leads the listener through a few reflection questions with pauses to think.

variants.name: Audio role-play
variants.description: Listeners hear a conversation acted out, sometimes in a good and a poor version, and judge what worked.

variants.name: Daily recap podcast
variants.description: A recording of a few minutes summarises each day of a programme and sets a question for the next day.

mechanics: Narrative learning; dual-channel boundaries; informal learning
cautions: Audio is a poor fit for dense new material, for anything that needs a diagram, and for skills that need practice. Use it for stories and viewpoints and follow it with a task.
theory: Narrative learning; dual-channel boundaries; informal learning
howTo: Pick content that works without pictures: a story, an interview or one argument.
Keep episodes to 10 to 20 minutes with one main point each.
Say the point at the start and again at the end. Listeners cannot skim back easily.
Finish with one question to think about or one thing to try.
Provide a transcript, and link the episode to a live discussion or a short task.
Record with a decent microphone in a quiet room. Poor sound loses listeners quickly.
time: 10 to 20 minutes per episode
group: Individuals, any number

name: Interactive video
description: A video that stops at set points and asks the viewer to answer a question, make a choice or click on something. What they see next can depend on their answer.
bestFor: Use it to show procedures and realistic situations to many people when you cannot be in the room with them.

variants.name: Branching video
variants.description: The viewer's choice decides which clip plays next, so different choices lead to different endings.

variants.name: Hotspot video
variants.description: The viewer clicks on parts of the picture to get more information or to spot a problem.

variants.name: Decision-point video
variants.description: The video stops at key moments and asks what to do, then carries on along one fixed path.

variants.name: Video with confidence checks
variants.description: After each answer the viewer rates how sure they were.

variants.name: Choose-the-expert-response video
variants.description: The viewer sees several responses to a situation and picks the one an expert would give.

variants.name: Annotated demonstration video
variants.description: A demonstration with labels and notes on screen that explain what the expert is doing and why.

variants.name: Video teardown
variants.description: The viewer watches a recorded performance and marks what was done well and badly, then compares with an expert's notes.

mechanics: Multimedia learning; retrieval; scenario-based learning
cautions: Adding clicks does not add learning. Every pause should ask for a decision the person will face at work.
theory: Multimedia learning; retrieval; scenario-based learning
howTo: Script the video around three to five decision points. A decision point is a moment where a real person would have to choose.
At each point, stop and ask one question with two to four believable options.
Give feedback on each option that shows what happens next, not only 'correct' or 'incorrect'.
Keep the whole thing under 10 minutes.
Test it with a few learners and remove any click that does not involve a decision.
Follow up with a live discussion or a practice task where you can.
time: 5 to 10 minutes to watch. Several days to script, film and build.
group: Individuals, any number

name: Adaptive learning system
description: A learning platform that changes what each person sees next according to how they answer. It skips what they know and gives more practice where they struggle.
bestFor: Use it for large groups who start with very different levels of knowledge of a well-defined subject.

variants.name: Diagnostic adaptive path
variants.description: A test at the start decides which parts each person can skip.

variants.name: Mastery-based adaptation
variants.description: People move on from a topic only after reaching a set score on it.

variants.name: Difficulty adaptation
variants.description: Questions get harder after right answers and easier after wrong ones.

variants.name: Content recommendation engine
variants.description: The platform suggests what to study next, based on role, history or results.

variants.name: Adaptive spacing engine
variants.description: The platform brings each item back for review at a time based on how well the person knew it.

variants.name: Adaptive scenario engine
variants.description: The work situations a person gets depend on the choices they made in earlier ones.

variants.name: Adaptive remediation
variants.description: A wrong answer triggers a short explanation and another go at a similar question.

mechanics: Mastery learning; knowledge tracing; adaptive testing
cautions: The adapting is only as good as the topic map and the questions behind it. If nobody can explain why the system chose a path, you cannot check it, so pilot first and keep a person reviewing the results.
theory: Mastery learning; knowledge tracing; adaptive testing
howTo: Check the subject suits it. It needs clear right and wrong answers and enough questions at every level.
Map the topics and which ones depend on which. The platform can only adapt along the map you give it.
Write or buy a large question bank, with several questions for each topic and level.
Ask the supplier how the platform decides what comes next, and ask to see the rules or the reports.
Run a pilot with 20 to 30 people and compare the platform's view of each person with a trainer's view.
Tell learners what data is collected and who can see it.
time: Weeks to set up. Learners use it for 10 to 20 minutes at a time.
group: Individuals, usually 50 or more to justify the cost

name: AI tutor
description: A chat-based AI tool that explains ideas, asks the learner questions, gives examples and responds to what the learner types, one person at a time.
bestFor: Use it to give each learner patient, on-demand explanation and practice questions between sessions.

variants.name: Socratic AI tutor
variants.description: The tutor answers with questions that lead the learner to work out the answer.

variants.name: Explain-it-differently tutor
variants.description: The learner can ask for the same idea again in simpler words or with a different example.

variants.name: Multimodal tutor
variants.description: The tutor works with speech, images or screenshots as well as text.

variants.name: Teach-back AI partner
variants.description: The learner explains the idea to the AI, which plays a beginner and asks questions about the gaps.

variants.name: AI question generator
variants.description: The AI writes practice questions from the course material for the learner to answer.

variants.name: AI misconception detector
variants.description: The AI looks at a learner's answers and points out the wrong idea that seems to lie behind them.

variants.name: AI study planner
variants.description: The AI turns a goal and the time available into a schedule of what to study and when.

variants.name: AI source-grounded tutor
variants.description: The tutor answers only from documents you have loaded and shows which passage each answer came from.

mechanics: Intelligent tutoring; scaffolding; feedback; Socratic dialogue
cautions: It can state wrong things with confidence, and learners can let it do the thinking for them. Tie it to checked sources, make people attempt an answer first, and keep confidential or personal data out of it.
theory: Intelligent tutoring; scaffolding; feedback; Socratic dialogue
howTo: Choose a tool the organisation has approved, and limit it to your course materials where the tool allows.
Write the instructions for the tutor: ask before telling, give hints before answers, and say so when a question is outside the sources.
Test it with 20 real learner questions, including awkward ones, and correct what it gets wrong.
Tell learners plainly that it can be wrong, that they should check anything important, and what they must not paste in.
Ask learners to attempt an answer before asking the tutor for one.
Read a sample of conversations each week, with learners' knowledge, to see where it misleads.
time: 5 to 15 minutes per use. 1 to 2 days to set up and test.
group: Individuals, any number

name: AI-generated personalised practice
description: You use an AI tool to write practice cases, questions and feedback that fit each learner's role, sector and level. A person checks them before learners see them.
bestFor: Use it when you need a lot of varied, realistic practice and the content changes too often to write it all by hand.

variants.name: Role-specific case generator
variants.description: The AI writes a case set in the learner's own role and sector.

variants.name: Difficulty-adjusting challenge generator
variants.description: The AI makes the next task harder or easier according to how the last one went.

variants.name: Personalised objection generator
variants.description: The AI writes the objections a learner's own customers are likely to raise, for sales or negotiation practice.

variants.name: Personalised quiz generator
variants.description: The AI writes recall questions from the material each learner has covered.

variants.name: Work-sample-to-practice converter
variants.description: A real piece of work, with names and details removed, is turned into a practice exercise.

variants.name: Scenario variation generator
variants.description: The AI produces several versions of one situation with details changed, so people cannot rely on memory.

variants.name: Personalised feedback loop
variants.description: The learner submits an answer, the AI comments against set criteria, and the learner revises and resubmits.

mechanics: Adaptive practice; deliberate practice; contextual variation
cautions: AI-written cases can be wrong, bland or unrealistic, and quality drifts between batches. Have an expert check each item against fixed criteria.
theory: Adaptive practice; deliberate practice; contextual variation
howTo: Write down what good practice material looks like: the skill, the level, the length and what a strong answer includes.
Give the AI tool that brief with two or three examples you wrote yourself. Use a tool the client has approved.
Generate a batch for one role. A subject expert reads every item and fixes or rejects it.
Keep the good items in a bank and tag each by role and difficulty.
In the session, give each person or pair the cases that match their role.
Review a sample every time the subject changes. Never paste real client or personal data into the tool.
time: 1 to 2 hours to produce and check a set. 10 to 20 minutes per practice task.
group: Individuals or pairs, any group size

name: Virtual reality training
description: Learners wear a headset and practise inside a computer-made 3D setting. The setting can show situations that would be dangerous, costly or impossible to set up for real.
bestFor: Use it for safety, equipment and spatial tasks where real practice is risky or expensive.

variants.name: 360-video VR experience
variants.description: The learner looks around inside a filmed real scene and cannot move through it or touch anything.

variants.name: Room-scale VR simulation
variants.description: The learner walks around a cleared physical space that matches the virtual one.

variants.name: Procedural VR rehearsal
variants.description: The learner carries out the steps of a procedure in order on virtual equipment.

variants.name: Soft-skills VR role-play
variants.description: The learner practises a conversation with a virtual character, such as an upset customer.

variants.name: Hazard-recognition VR
variants.description: The learner looks round a virtual workplace and points out the dangers.

variants.name: Collaborative multi-user VR
variants.description: Several learners share the same virtual space and work on a task together.

variants.name: VR with haptic feedback
variants.description: Gloves or controllers add touch, such as vibration or resistance, to the experience.

variants.name: VR assessment
variants.description: The system records what the learner does in the scenario and scores it against a standard.

mechanics: Embodied cognition; presence; experiential learning
cautions: Headsets are costly, some people feel sick in them and some cannot use them at all. Use VR only when the task needs it, not because it is new, and always offer another way in.
theory: Embodied cognition; presence; experiential learning
howTo: Check that the task needs it. Use VR when being in the space matters and the real thing cannot be practised safely or cheaply.
Start with a five-minute orientation so that people learn the controls before the task begins.
Keep each turn to 10 to 15 minutes. Have people seated or in a clear space with a helper nearby.
Have an alternative ready, such as the same scenario on a screen, for anyone who feels unwell or cannot wear a headset.
Debrief straight afterwards: what they noticed, what they decided and what they would do in the real place.
Clean the headsets between users and allow changeover time.
time: 10 to 15 minutes per person in the headset, plus a 10-minute debrief
group: One person per headset. Rotate small groups of 3 or 4.

name: Augmented reality guidance
description: Instructions, labels or arrows appear on a phone, tablet or headset screen, laid over the camera view of the real equipment the person is working on.
bestFor: Use it for maintenance, assembly and field tasks where people need step-by-step guidance on the object in front of them.

variants.name: Phone-based AR guide
variants.description: The overlay appears on the user's own phone, held up to the equipment.

variants.name: Tablet AR procedure
variants.description: A tablet on a stand or in the hand shows each step over the camera view.

variants.name: Wearable AR instructions
variants.description: Smart glasses or a headset show the steps and leave both hands free.

variants.name: Remote-expert AR support
variants.description: An expert elsewhere sees the worker's camera view and draws on it to show what to do.

variants.name: AR object identification
variants.description: Pointing the camera at a part brings up its name and details.

variants.name: AR safety overlay
variants.description: Hazards, exclusion zones or isolation points are highlighted in the view of the real place.

variants.name: AR learning trail
variants.description: Markers around a site each open a short explanation of what you are looking at.

mechanics: Situated cognition; performance support; embodied learning
cautions: Narrow views, heavy headsets, flat batteries and poor signal get in the way on site. Start small on devices people own, and never make AR the only source of safety-critical steps.
theory: Situated cognition; performance support; embodied learning
howTo: Pick one procedure on one piece of equipment where people often need to check the manual.
Break it into steps and decide what the overlay shows at each one: an arrow, a label or a short clip.
Start with phones or tablets people already have before buying headsets.
Test it at the real place of work, checking for lighting, gloves, noise and signal.
Watch three users follow it and fix every step where the overlay hides the work or lags.
Keep a paper or on-screen copy for when the device fails.
time: Follows the length of the task. Weeks to build one procedure.
group: Individuals at the equipment

name: Mixed-reality simulation
description: Learners work with real objects and computer-made ones together in the same space. A headset shows virtual parts placed onto real equipment, and the two respond to each other.
bestFor: Use it for team practice on large or complex equipment, when a supplier or client already has the kit.

variants.name: Shared holographic simulation
variants.description: Everyone wearing a headset sees and handles the same 3D model in the middle of the room.

variants.name: Physical-digital equipment simulation
variants.description: Real controls or a mock-up are linked to software that responds as the real machine would.

variants.name: Mixed-reality team exercise
variants.description: A team works through an incident with virtual events appearing in their real workspace.

variants.name: Spatial data visualisation lab
variants.description: Data is shown as a 3D model that people can walk round and discuss.

variants.name: Remote mixed-reality collaboration
variants.description: People in different places see the same virtual object and each other's pointers.

mechanics: Embodied cognition; distributed cognition; presence
cautions: It is expensive, and the evidence that it beats simpler formats is mixed. Choose only as much realism as the learning aim needs, and budget for support staff.
theory: Embodied cognition; distributed cognition; presence
howTo: Confirm the aim and ask whether a cheaper format, such as a physical model or a tabletop exercise, would do the same job.
Work with a specialist supplier. Very few trainers build this themselves.
Brief the team on the task and their roles, and allow 10 minutes to get used to the equipment.
Run the scenario for 15 to 20 minutes while a facilitator watches and takes notes.
Debrief for at least as long as the scenario ran: what happened, why, and what carries over to the real job.
Have a plan for technical failure, such as a paper version of the same scenario.
time: 45 to 60 minutes with briefing and debrief
group: Teams of 2 to 6 per set-up

name: Serious game
description: A game, on a table or a screen, built so that playing it teaches something specific. Players make choices, see what follows and try again.
bestFor: Use it when people need to see how the parts of a system affect each other, or need repeated decision practice in a form they will stay with.

variants.name: Cooperative serious game
variants.description: All the players work together against the game and win or lose as one.

variants.name: Competitive serious game
variants.description: Teams or players compete against each other for the best result.

variants.name: Systems game
variants.description: Players run part of a system and discover how their choices affect the other parts.

variants.name: Resource-allocation game
variants.description: Players divide limited money, time or people between competing needs.

variants.name: Decision-consequence game
variants.description: Each choice changes what happens next, and the effects build up over the rounds.

variants.name: Narrative quest
variants.description: Players follow a story and solve a task at each stage to move forward.

variants.name: Card-based learning game
variants.description: The game is played with a deck of cards carrying situations, roles or actions.

variants.name: Board-based business game
variants.description: Teams move through rounds on a printed board that represents a company or market.

variants.name: Digital strategy game
variants.description: The game runs on computers, and the software works out the results of each choice.

variants.name: Team mission game
variants.description: A team has a set time to complete a shared mission made up of linked tasks.

mechanics: Game-based learning; experiential learning; systems feedback
cautions: A game can be fun and teach nothing if winning does not depend on the skill you are after. Competition also puts some people off, so check the fit and always debrief.
theory: Game-based learning; experiential learning; systems feedback
howTo: Start from the learning aim and the decisions you want people to practise. Choose or design a game where those decisions drive the result.
Play it yourself with a test group first. Time it and note where the rules confuse.
Explain the rules in under five minutes and play one practice round.
Run the game for 20 to 40 minutes. Watch what teams do and write down moments to raise afterwards.
Debrief for at least 15 minutes: 'What happened? Why? Where do you see this at work?'
Decide beforehand whether to keep score, and prefer team play if competition might shut some people out.
time: 45 to 75 minutes, including the debrief
group: Teams of 3 to 5, any number of teams

name: Business simulation
description: Teams run a simplified company or market for several rounds. Each round they make decisions on price, staff or investment, then see the results before deciding again.
bestFor: Use it to teach strategy, finance and how decisions in one part of a business affect the rest.

variants.name: Strategy simulation
variants.description: Teams set the direction of a company over several years and compete for market share.

variants.name: Market-entry simulation
variants.description: Teams decide whether, where and how to launch in a new market.

variants.name: Financial simulation
variants.description: Teams manage cash, costs and investment and read the accounts after each round.

variants.name: Supply-chain simulation
variants.description: Teams place orders and manage stock along a chain and see how delays build up.

variants.name: Operating-model simulation
variants.description: Teams redesign how work, roles and handovers are organised and see the effect on cost and service.

variants.name: Cyber-risk simulation
variants.description: Teams decide how much to spend on security and how to respond when attacks hit.

variants.name: Customer-experience simulation
variants.description: Teams make service choices and watch customer satisfaction and loyalty change.

variants.name: Sustainability simulation
variants.description: Teams balance profit with environmental and social targets.

variants.name: Resource-allocation simulation
variants.description: Teams divide a fixed budget or headcount between departments or projects.
