variants.name: Portfolio simulation
variants.description: Teams choose which projects or products to fund, continue or stop.

mechanics: Experiential learning; systems dynamics; feedback loops
cautions: The model is built on someone's assumptions, and teams can learn to beat the game without learning the business. Name the assumptions and spend real time on the debrief.
theory: Experiential learning; systems dynamics; feedback loops
howTo: Choose a simulation whose decisions match what your learners decide, or could decide, at work. Play it through yourself first.
Brief the teams for 15 minutes on the company, the rules and what counts as success.
Run three to five rounds of 20 to 30 minutes. Give out the results after each round.
Pause after every round for five minutes so that teams can say what they expected and what happened.
Hold a full debrief of 30 to 45 minutes at the end, linking what teams did to their real business.
Say out loud which simplifications the model makes, so nobody treats it as the truth.
time: Half a day to two days
group: Teams of 3 to 5, with 3 to 6 teams

name: Tabletop exercise
description: A group sits round a table and talks through how it would respond to a made-up incident. A facilitator reveals the incident in stages, and nobody leaves the room to do anything.
bestFor: Use it to test a crisis, security or continuity plan and to make sure people know their roles.

variants.name: Cyber incident tabletop
variants.description: The scenario is a cyber attack, such as ransomware.

variants.name: Crisis communications tabletop
variants.description: The exercise centres on what to say, to whom and when, as events unfold.

variants.name: Business continuity tabletop
variants.description: A site, system or supplier is lost, and the group works out how to keep operating.

variants.name: AI governance tabletop
variants.description: An AI system produces a harmful or wrong result, and the group works out who is accountable and what to do.

variants.name: Data-breach tabletop
variants.description: Personal data has been exposed, and the group covers containment, notification and customers.

variants.name: Reputation-risk tabletop
variants.description: A damaging story is spreading in the press or on social media.

variants.name: Client escalation tabletop
variants.description: A major client complaint is escalating, and the account team works out its response.

variants.name: Regulatory-response tabletop
variants.description: A regulator opens an enquiry or announces an inspection.

variants.name: Product-failure tabletop
variants.description: A product fault or recall has to be handled.

variants.name: Third-party failure tabletop
variants.description: A key supplier or partner fails, and the group works through the knock-on effects.

mechanics: Simulation; shared mental models; team cognition
cautions: Talking a plan through is easier than carrying it out, so a smooth exercise can make people overconfident. Add time pressure, record the gaps and follow up on the fixes.
theory: Simulation; shared mental models; team cognition
howTo: Write a realistic scenario with three or four 'injects'. An inject is a new piece of information that changes the situation.
Invite the people who would really be involved. Ask each to answer from their real role.
Read the opening. Ask 'What do you do first? Who decides? Who do you tell?' Allow 15 minutes.
Reveal each inject in turn, with 10 to 15 minutes of discussion on each. Add a time limit to at least one of them.
Have a note-taker record every gap, unclear role and missing contact.
Close with 20 minutes on the top three fixes, each with an owner and a date.
time: 90 minutes to 2 hours
group: 6 to 12 people from the roles involved

name: Field study / contextual immersion
description: Learners go to the place where the work or the customer is. They watch what happens, talk to the people there, and bring back notes and examples to make sense of together.
bestFor: Use it when people need to understand a customer, a user or an operation at first hand before they design or decide anything.

variants.name: Customer observation
variants.description: Learners watch customers using the product or service without stepping in.

variants.name: Service safari
variants.description: Learners go through a service as a customer would and note each step.

variants.name: Contextual interview
variants.description: Learners interview someone at their place of work while that person does the task.

variants.name: Workplace ethnography
variants.description: Learners spend days or weeks in a workplace to understand its habits and unwritten rules.

variants.name: Diary study immersion
variants.description: People being studied keep a diary for a week or two, and learners read the entries and discuss them.

variants.name: Shop-along
variants.description: A learner goes with a customer on a shopping trip and asks about their choices.

variants.name: Ride-along
variants.description: A learner travels with a field worker for a day and watches their visits.

variants.name: Competitive experience safari
variants.description: Learners try a competitor's product or service as customers and compare it with their own.

variants.name: Community immersion
variants.description: Learners spend time in a community they serve, hosted by people who live or work there.

mechanics: Situated cognition; experiential learning; ethnography
cautions: People see what they expected to see, and those being watched may feel inspected. Get consent, record what was seen separately from what you think it means, and compare notes across pairs.
theory: Situated cognition; experiential learning; ethnography
howTo: Agree what you want to find out, and write three or four things to look for.
Arrange access and consent. Tell the people being visited who is coming, why, and what will be recorded.
Brief the learners for 15 minutes: watch first, ask open questions, write down what you see and hear, and do not judge yet.
Send them in pairs for 1 to 3 hours. One person asks and the other takes notes.
Back in the room, each pair shares three observations on sticky notes. Group them and look for patterns.
Ask 'What surprised you?' and 'What does this change about our plan?'
time: Half a day, including briefing and debrief
group: Pairs, in a group of 6 to 12

name: Outdoor experiential learning
description: Teams do a practical task outdoors, such as building, finding a route or solving a physical puzzle. They then sit down to discuss how they worked together and what that says about work.
bestFor: Use it to give a team a shared experience of planning, communicating and leading under uncertainty that it can then examine.

variants.name: Low-ropes team challenge
variants.description: Teams solve physical puzzles on ropes and beams close to the ground, run by a qualified instructor.

variants.name: Navigation challenge
variants.description: Teams find their way between points with a map and limited information.

variants.name: Expedition learning
variants.description: A group makes a trip of a day or more on foot or by boat and reflects each evening.

variants.name: Outdoor problem solving
variants.description: Teams solve a practical puzzle outside using simple kit such as ropes, planks or buckets.

variants.name: Nature-based leadership reflection
variants.description: People spend time alone or in pairs in a natural setting, thinking about a leadership question.

variants.name: Accessible outdoor collaboration
variants.description: The task is designed so that people of any mobility can take a full part, on flat ground near facilities.

variants.name: Survival scenario with debrief
variants.description: Teams rank items or make decisions for an imagined survival situation, then compare their reasoning.

mechanics: Experiential learning; self-efficacy; team development
cautions: It can shut people out on physical or cultural grounds, and without a strong debrief it is only a day out. Design for everyone and give the debrief as much care as the activity.
theory: Experiential learning; self-efficacy; team development
howTo: Pick a task with a clear link to work, such as planning with limited information. Check that everyone can take part.
Ask about access needs and health beforehand. Offer real roles that do not depend on physical ability, such as planner or observer.
Brief the task, the safety rules and the time limit in 5 minutes.
Run the task for 20 to 40 minutes. Watch and take notes without helping.
Debrief for at least 20 minutes: 'What happened? What helped? What got in the way? Where do we do this at work?'
Each person writes down one thing they will do differently at work.
time: 60 to 90 minutes, including the debrief
group: Teams of 5 to 8

name: Walking learning / learning walk
description: People walk together, usually in pairs, while they discuss a set question or observe something along the route. The group then gathers to share what came up.
bestFor: Use it for reflection and for pairs getting to know each other, especially after a long stretch of sitting.

variants.name: Paired coaching walk
variants.description: One person talks through a challenge while the other only asks questions, then they swap halfway.

variants.name: Observation walk
variants.description: People walk through a workplace or area with a list of things to look for.

variants.name: Gallery learning walk
variants.description: The group walks round work or posters on the walls and leaves comments on each.

variants.name: System walk
variants.description: The group follows a process through the building from start to finish, stopping at each stage.

variants.name: Customer journey walk
variants.description: The group follows the route a customer takes and notes what the customer would see and feel at each point.

variants.name: Silent reflection walk
variants.description: People walk alone and in silence with one question, then write for a few minutes.

variants.name: Walk-and-talk mentoring
variants.description: A mentor and mentee hold their regular conversation while walking.

mechanics: Embodied cognition; attention restoration; reflective practice
cautions: Not everyone can or wants to walk, and weather and privacy can spoil it. Always have a real alternative and keep sensitive topics for indoors.
theory: Embodied cognition; attention restoration; reflective practice
howTo: Plan a safe, step-free route of 15 to 25 minutes. Walk it yourself first.
Offer a seated or indoor option as an equal choice.
Set one clear question, for example 'What from this morning will you use first, and what might stop you?'
Pair people up and say when to be back. Suggest they swap who is talking at the halfway point.
Remind people not to discuss confidential matters where they can be overheard.
When everyone is back, take one point from each pair and write them up.
time: 20 to 30 minutes
group: Pairs or threes, any group size

name: Residential learning retreat
description: A group goes away together for two or more days, staying overnight. Time away from daily work is used for focused learning, practice, reflection and getting to know each other.
bestFor: Use it to start or finish a long programme, or for work that needs unbroken time and trust between people.

variants.name: Executive residency
variants.description: Senior leaders go away to work on strategy and their own leadership.

variants.name: Skills bootcamp residency
variants.description: Several intensive days of practice are spent on one skill set.

variants.name: Creative retreat
variants.description: Time and space are given to making and exploring ideas, with few fixed sessions.

variants.name: Leadership retreat
variants.description: Leaders reflect on how they lead, get feedback and practise.

variants.name: Innovation retreat
variants.description: A team works on new ideas for products or services away from the office.

variants.name: Learning festival retreat
variants.description: Many short sessions run in parallel, and people choose which to attend.

variants.name: Studio residency
variants.description: People work on their own projects side by side, with regular critique from the group.

variants.name: Field-immersion retreat
variants.description: The group stays near a customer, site or community and learns from visits.

variants.name: Cohort launch retreat
variants.description: The retreat opens a longer programme and builds the group.

variants.name: Capstone retreat
variants.description: The retreat closes a programme, and people present what they have done and plan what comes next.

mechanics: Adult learning; cognitive load management; social learning; attention restoration
cautions: The intensity makes people feel changed, and the feeling fades once they are back at work. Plan the follow-up before you go, protect sleep and make sure nobody is shut out by the venue or the timetable.
theory: Adult learning; cognitive load management; social learning; attention restoration
howTo: Fix the aim and what people will have made or decided by the end. Tell them before they arrive.
Ask about access, diet, caring duties and sleep needs beforehand. Choose a venue everyone can use.
Plan each day around energy: hard thinking in the morning, practice after lunch and lighter work late in the day. Finish by early evening.
Build in breaks, time outdoors and free time, and keep evenings optional.
Spend the last half day on what people will do back at work, who will support them and what might stop them.
Book a follow-up call two to four weeks later, and brief managers before the retreat.
time: 2 to 4 days
group: 8 to 20 people

name: Silent reflection / solo integration
description: A quiet period with no new content. Each person works alone to write down what they have learned, what it means for them and what they will do.
bestFor: Use it after a dense block of input or at the end of a day, so that people sort out their thinking before moving on.

variants.name: Guided journalling
variants.description: People write answers to a series of prompts that you read out one at a time.

variants.name: Decision journal
variants.description: People write down a decision they face, the options and the reasons for each.

variants.name: Future-self letter
variants.description: People write a letter to themselves to open in three months, saying what they intend to have done.

variants.name: Solo synthesis map
variants.description: People draw a one-page map that links the main ideas of the programme to their own work.

variants.name: Silent nature reflection
variants.description: People spend the time alone outdoors with one question and write on their return.

variants.name: Personal manifesto
variants.description: People write a short statement of the principles they will work by.

variants.name: Commitment contract
variants.description: People write one specific commitment, sign it and give a copy to a partner who will check on it.

variants.name: Private video reflection
variants.description: People record a short video to themselves on their phone, to watch later.

mechanics: Consolidation; metacognition; reflection
cautions: Some people find silence uncomfortable or do not know what to do with it. Give clear prompts, keep it short at first and allow drawing, typing or speaking quietly into a phone as alternatives.
theory: Consolidation; metacognition; reflection
howTo: Say why you are doing it and how long it will last. 10 to 20 minutes is enough.
Give two or three written prompts, for example 'What matters most from today? What will I do first? What am I unsure about?'
Let people choose where to sit, or go outside. Phones and laptops stay away unless needed for writing.
Keep the silence yourself. Do not fill it or walk round the room.
Give a two-minute warning before the end.
Invite people to share one line with a neighbour, and make it clear they can decline.
time: 10 to 20 minutes
group: Individuals, any group size

name: Transformative learning dialogue
description: A carefully facilitated conversation in which people examine a belief they hold about their work or role, hear views that challenge it, and consider whether it still holds.
bestFor: Use it with people moving into a very different role, or facing questions of ethics and values, once the group trusts each other.

variants.name: Disorienting-dilemma dialogue
variants.description: The session starts from an experience that did not fit what people expected and asks what it shows.

variants.name: Critical assumption audit
variants.description: People list the assumptions behind a decision or habit and test each one against evidence.

variants.name: Perspective transformation circle
variants.description: The group sits in a circle, and each person describes a view they once held and what changed it.

variants.name: Identity transition dialogue
variants.description: People moving into a new role, such as first-time managers, discuss what they must let go of and take on.

variants.name: Values conflict dialogue
variants.description: People work through a situation where two things they value pull in different directions.

variants.name: Threshold concept seminar
variants.description: The group studies one hard idea that, once understood, changes how the rest of the subject looks.

tierRaw: B/C - Conditional and contested in parts
mechanics: Mezirow transformative learning
cautions: Do not push people to disclose, and do not promise that anyone will be changed. Go at the group's pace, let people pass, and know where to refer someone who becomes distressed.
theory: Mezirow transformative learning
howTo: Use it only with a group that already has trust and agreed ground rules. Remind people they choose what to share.
Start from a real situation where an assumption was shaken, such as a case, a story or a participant's own example.
Ask each person to write for five minutes: 'What did I assume here? Where did that assumption come from?'
In threes, each person shares for five minutes while the others ask questions only and give no advice.
Bring in a different view, such as a guest, a reading or data, and ask 'What would have to be true for this view to make sense?'
Close with private writing on what, if anything, has shifted. Do not ask anyone to announce a change.
time: 60 to 90 minutes
group: 8 to 12, working in threes

name: Critical incident method
description: A person or group picks one real event that mattered and takes it apart: what they noticed, what they decided, what they assumed and what else they could have done.
bestFor: Use it to build judgement in leadership, safety and client work from people's own experience.

variants.name: Critical incident interview
variants.description: One person is interviewed in depth about an event while the others listen.

variants.name: Incident timeline reconstruction
variants.description: The group draws the event as a timeline and marks each decision on it.

variants.name: Decision autopsy
variants.description: The group examines one decision that turned out badly and separates what was knowable then from what is known now.

variants.name: Near-miss review
variants.description: The event is one that almost went wrong, studied for what saved it.

variants.name: Success incident analysis
variants.description: The event is one that went well, studied for what made it work.

variants.name: Client incident clinic
variants.description: People bring a difficult client event and the group helps to analyse it.

variants.name: Leadership incident reflection
variants.description: A leader writes about and reflects on a moment that tested them.

mechanics: Critical incident technique; reflective practice; naturalistic decision making
cautions: Memory tidies events up afterwards, so accounts are partial and kind to the teller. Check against records or other people where you can, and keep the focus on decisions, not blame.
theory: Critical incident technique; reflective practice; naturalistic decision making
howTo: Ask each person to choose a real event from their work that went notably well or badly, and that they are willing to discuss.
They write it up in 10 minutes: what happened, in order, with no explanation yet.
In pairs or threes, the listener asks 'What did you notice at that point? What did you decide? What were you assuming?'
Together they find the two or three moments where a different choice was possible, and what would have prompted it.
Check the account against any facts available, such as emails, logs or another person's view.
Each person writes one rule of thumb to take from it. Share these round the group.
time: 45 to 60 minutes
group: Pairs or threes, in a group of 6 to 12

name: Premortem
description: Before a project starts, the team imagines that it has already failed. Each person writes down why, and the team then plans how to prevent the most likely causes.
bestFor: Use it at the planning stage, when a team is confident and may be missing risks.

variants.name: Project premortem
variants.description: The standard version, run on a project plan before work begins.

variants.name: Learning transfer premortem
variants.description: The group imagines that the training did not change anything at work and asks why.

variants.name: Client-engagement premortem
variants.description: The team imagines that a client engagement went wrong and plans against the causes.

variants.name: AI-risk premortem
variants.description: The team imagines that an AI tool it is introducing has caused harm or failed, and works back to the causes.

variants.name: Career experiment premortem
variants.description: One person imagines that a career move they are planning has not worked out, and lists why.

variants.name: Team failure premortem
variants.description: The team imagines that it has stopped working well together and names what led there.

mechanics: Prospective hindsight; debiasing; mental simulation
cautions: It can become a long list of worries that nobody acts on. Vote, pick a few, give each one an owner, and end on what the team will do.
theory: Prospective hindsight; debiasing; mental simulation
howTo: Describe the plan in two minutes. Then say 'It is a year from now and this has failed badly. Write down why.'
Everyone writes reasons alone and in silence for five minutes.
Go round the room taking one reason from each person until all are on the board. Do not debate yet.
Group similar reasons. Give each person three votes for the most likely and most damaging.
For the top three to five, agree one action to prevent each or to spot it early, with an owner.
Add the actions to the project plan and look at them again at the first review.
time: 30 to 45 minutes
group: The project team, 4 to 12 people

name: Red teaming
description: A separate group is given the job of attacking a plan, product or decision as an opponent or critic would, in order to find weaknesses before they matter.
bestFor: Use it to test a strategy, a security set-up, an AI system or any important decision before you commit to it.

variants.name: Red-team/blue-team exercise
variants.description: One team attacks and another defends, often over several rounds.

variants.name: Assumption attack
variants.description: The red team lists the assumptions the plan depends on and argues that each one is false.

variants.name: Adversarial review
variants.description: A reviewer is asked to find every flaw they can in a document or design.

variants.name: Prompt red teaming
variants.description: People try to make an AI system give harmful, wrong or off-limits answers, to find its weak points.

variants.name: Cyber red team
variants.description: Authorised specialists try to break into systems as an attacker would.

variants.name: Strategy red team
variants.description: A group plays a competitor or critic and responds to your strategy.

variants.name: Devil’s advocate rotation
variants.description: One person in each meeting is assigned to argue against the proposal, and the job passes round.

variants.name: Pre-publication challenge panel
variants.description: A small panel questions a report or decision hard before it is released.

mechanics: Cognitive conflict; adversarial testing; error detection
cautions: Attacks can turn personal, or the owners get defensive and nothing changes. Set rules, keep the challenge on the work, rotate the roles and record what changes as a result.
theory: Cognitive conflict; adversarial testing; error detection
howTo: Agree the scope and the rules: what is being tested, what is off limits, and that the attack is on the work, never the people.
Split into the owners of the plan (blue) and the challengers (red). Give the red team 20 to 30 minutes to prepare alone.
The red team presents its three to five strongest attacks. The blue team listens and does not defend yet.
The blue team responds to each one with 'accept', 'fix' or 'disagree, because'.
Together, list the changes to make, with owners.
Close by thanking the red team and stepping out of the roles. Swap sides next time.
time: 60 to 90 minutes for a workshop version
group: 8 to 12, split into two teams

name: Future scenario planning
description: Teams build a few different, believable pictures of how the future could turn out. They test their plans against each one and agree which early signs to watch for.
bestFor: Use it with leadership teams that face real uncertainty and need a strategy that holds up in more than one future.

variants.name: Two-by-two scenarios
variants.description: Two uncertain forces are crossed to make four futures.

variants.name: Three-horizons exploration
variants.description: The group maps what is fading now, what is emerging and what might replace both in the long term.

variants.name: Wind-tunnelling strategy test
variants.description: An existing strategy is tested against each scenario to see where it fails.

variants.name: Backcasting
variants.description: The group starts from a future it wants and works backwards to the steps needed to get there.

variants.name: Future wheel
variants.description: One change is written in the centre, and the group maps its direct effects and then the effects of those.

variants.name: Signals-to-scenarios lab
variants.description: The group collects small signs of change that are happening now and builds scenarios from them.

variants.name: Role-play in future worlds
variants.description: People act out a meeting or decision as if they were living in one of the scenarios.

variants.name: No-regret moves workshop
variants.description: The group picks out the actions that make sense in every scenario.

tierRaw: D/B - Practitioner framework with research support
mechanics: Prospective thinking; systems thinking; mental simulation
cautions: People treat the scenario they like best as a forecast. Keep saying that these are possibilities, and test the plan against all of them.
theory: Prospective thinking; systems thinking; mental simulation
howTo: Set the question and the time frame, for example 'Our market in five years'.
List the forces that could shape it. Choose the two that are both most uncertain and most important.
Make a two-by-two grid from those two forces, giving four futures. Give each a short name.
Small groups take one future each and spend 20 to 30 minutes describing a day in that world.
Test the current strategy against each future: what works, what breaks, and what works in all four.
Agree two or three early signs to watch for each future, and who will watch them.
time: Half a day to a full day
group: 8 to 16, in four groups

name: Appreciative inquiry summit
description: A large-group event, often one to three days, that moves through four stages. People find what already works, picture what could be, design how to get there and commit to actions.
bestFor: Use it for culture and organisation change, when you want many people involved in shaping what comes next.

variants.name: Discovery interviews
variants.description: Pairs interview each other about their best experiences of the topic, used alone or as the first stage.

variants.name: Dream workshop
variants.description: A session where groups picture and present the future they want.

variants.name: Design summit
variants.description: A session that turns the picture of the future into concrete proposals.

variants.name: Destiny commitments
variants.description: A closing session where people commit publicly to actions and form groups to carry them out.

variants.name: Whole-system summit
variants.description: Everyone with a stake, including customers and partners, is in the room for all four stages.

variants.name: Strengths-story exchange
variants.description: People swap short stories of the team at its best and list what the stories have in common.

mechanics: Social constructionism; positive organisational scholarship
cautions: A focus on strengths can silence real problems and questions of power. Make room to name what is not working, and make sure leaders are ready to act on what comes out.
theory: Social constructionism; positive organisational scholarship
howTo: Agree a positive, specific topic with a planning group drawn from across the organisation, for example 'Great handovers'.
Discover: pairs interview each other about a time the topic went really well, for 20 minutes each way.
Small groups share the stories and pull out what made those times possible.
Dream: groups picture and present the organisation as it would be if those conditions were normal.
Design: groups write concrete proposals for what would have to change.
Commit (often called Destiny): people sign up to actions and working groups, with a follow-up date.
time: 1 to 3 days. A half-day version for one team is possible.
group: 30 to several hundred, in tables of 6 to 8

name: Train-the-trainer
description: A programme that prepares people to deliver a course themselves. They learn the content, practise teaching it, get feedback, and are supported through their first deliveries.
bestFor: Use it to roll out one standard programme across many sites or teams through local trainers.

variants.name: Facilitator certification
variants.description: Trainers must pass an observed delivery against a standard before they run the course alone.

variants.name: Practice-teach-practice
variants.description: Trainers practise a section, teach it to real learners, then practise again using the feedback.

variants.name: Cascade trainer pathway
variants.description: Master trainers train local trainers, who then train the end learners.

variants.name: Lead-facilitator apprenticeship
variants.description: A new trainer works beside a lead trainer over several deliveries and takes on more each time.

variants.name: Co-facilitation practicum
variants.description: Two trainers deliver together, and each gives the other feedback afterwards.

variants.name: Trainer calibration clinic
variants.description: Trainers watch the same recording, score it separately and compare, so that they judge to the same standard.

mechanics: Social learning; modelling; fidelity; communities of practice
cautions: The course gets weaker each time it is passed on. Give trainers a full guide, watch them teach before they go solo and check quality afterwards.
theory: Social learning; modelling; fidelity; communities of practice
howTo: Choose trainers who know the subject and want to teach. Have them attend the course as learners first.
Walk through the facilitator guide and explain why each activity is there, not only what to do.
Each person teaches a 10 to 15 minute section to the group and gets feedback against a checklist.
Repeat with a harder section, including handling questions and running the debrief.
For their first real delivery, pair each new trainer with an experienced one. Observe and debrief.
Keep the trainers in touch through a shared channel and regular check-ins, and observe each trainer again from time to time.
time: 2 to 3 days, plus observed first deliveries
group: 6 to 12 new trainers

name: Capability academy
description: A long-running programme for one role or skill area, run inside an organisation. It combines an entry assessment, courses, practice, real projects, coaching and a recognised end point.
bestFor: Use it when an organisation needs to build one skill area across many people over a year or more.

variants.name: Role academy
variants.description: The academy is built around one job, such as sales manager.

variants.name: Skill academy
variants.description: The academy is built around one skill, such as data analysis, for people in many roles.

variants.name: Leadership academy
variants.description: The academy develops managers and leaders at several levels.

variants.name: AI academy
variants.description: The academy teaches staff to use AI tools well and safely in their own work.

variants.name: Client-facing academy
variants.description: The academy is for people who work directly with clients and builds consulting and relationship skills.

variants.name: Technical academy
variants.description: The academy builds depth in a technical field such as engineering or cloud.

variants.name: Cross-functional academy
variants.description: People from different departments learn together about a shared process or goal.

variants.name: Academy with residency and workplace capstone
variants.description: The academy includes a residential block and ends with a real project presented to sponsors.

tierRaw: B/D - System design with supported components
mechanics: Expertise development; transfer; learning ecosystems; communities of practice
cautions: Many academies end up as a library of courses with a logo. Without levels, real work and assessment, it is only a catalogue.
theory: Expertise development; transfer; learning ecosystems; communities of practice
howTo: Define the role or skill, and describe what good looks like at each level in terms of what people do.
Assess people at the start so that each one begins at the right level.
Build a path for each level: a small amount of teaching, a lot of practice, a real project and coaching.
Involve managers. They agree the project and review progress.
Set an assessment at the end of each level that is based on real work.
Review each year what is used and what is not, and cut what is not.
time: Months to set up. Learners spend 6 to 12 months per level.
group: Cohorts of 12 to 20, repeated across the organisation

name: Mastery learning
description: People move on to the next unit only after they have shown they can do the current one to a set standard. Those who fall short get targeted help and another attempt.
bestFor: Use it where later learning depends on earlier learning, or where a mistake on the job would be serious.

variants.name: Mastery checkpoint cycle
variants.description: Each unit ends with a check that must be passed before the next unit opens.

variants.name: Corrective instruction loop
variants.description: After a failed check the learner gets a different form of teaching on what they missed.

variants.name: Competency gate
variants.description: A single pass or fail assessment stands before a higher-risk task or stage.

variants.name: Test-reteach-retest
variants.description: The group is tested, the weak points are retaught and a second test follows.

variants.name: Variable-time mastery path
variants.description: The standard is fixed and the time is not, so each person takes as long as they need.

variants.name: Mastery through performance
variants.description: The check is a real or simulated task that is observed, not a written test.

mechanics: Bloom mastery learning; formative assessment; feedback
cautions: It takes more time and more assessment material than a fixed timetable, and a weak standard makes the whole thing pointless. Define the standard carefully and budget the time.
theory: Bloom mastery learning; formative assessment; feedback
howTo: Break the course into units and define the standard for each, such as 'handles the call without missing any of the five checks'.
Teach the unit, then run a short check against the standard.
People who pass move on or take an extension task.
People who do not pass get different help from the first time, such as a new explanation, a worked example or coaching.
They take a second, different version of the check. Repeat until they pass.
Plan the extra time and the spare versions of each check beforehand.
time: Varies from person to person. Allow about a fifth extra time for help and second attempts.
group: Individuals within a group of any size

name: Portfolio-based learning and assessment
description: Over months, learners collect examples of their real work, feedback they received and their own notes on what they learned. The collection is then judged against set criteria.
bestFor: Use it to assess skills that show up in real work over time and cannot be judged in a single test.

variants.name: Evidence portfolio
variants.description: A collection of work samples is matched to each required skill.

variants.name: Reflective portfolio
variants.description: The weight is on the learner's written reflections about each piece.

variants.name: Project portfolio
variants.description: The portfolio documents one or more complete projects from start to finish.

variants.name: Video performance portfolio
variants.description: The portfolio holds recordings of the learner doing the skill, such as presenting or coaching.

variants.name: Client-impact portfolio
variants.description: The portfolio shows the results of work for clients, with their feedback.

variants.name: Credential portfolio
variants.description: The portfolio is submitted to gain a qualification or professional status.

variants.name: Peer-reviewed portfolio
variants.description: Other learners review and comment on the portfolio against the criteria.

mechanics: Authentic assessment; metacognition; reflective practice
cautions: A thick, polished folder can hide weak skill. Limit the number of pieces, judge against a rubric and confirm that the work is the learner's own.
theory: Authentic assessment; metacognition; reflective practice
howTo: Define the criteria and what counts as evidence for each. Give learners the rubric at the start.
Ask for a small number of pieces, for example five, each with a short note on what it shows and what they would change.
Schedule two or three reviews along the way with a coach or a peer.
Require some evidence that another person can confirm, such as a manager's sign-off, a recording or client feedback.
Have two people judge the final portfolio against the rubric and compare their views.
End with a conversation where the learner talks through one piece.
time: Built over 3 to 12 months. 30 to 60 minutes to review each one.
group: Individuals, with a reviewer or coach

name: Credential / certification pathway
description: A programme that ends in a formal assessment against a standard. Passing gives a certificate, badge or qualification that the employer or an outside body recognises.
bestFor: Use it when people or employers need proof of a skill, for technical depth, client trust or career progress.

variants.name: Knowledge certification
variants.description: A written or online exam shows what the person knows.

variants.name: Performance certification
variants.description: The person is observed doing the task to a set standard.

variants.name: Stackable microcredential
variants.description: Small credentials each cover one skill and can be added together into a larger one.

variants.name: Digital badge pathway
variants.description: Each step earns an online badge that can be shown on a profile and checked by others.

variants.name: Skills passport
variants.description: One record lists the skills a person has been assessed on and goes with them between roles or employers.

variants.name: Practical accreditation
variants.description: An outside body confirms that the person or the programme meets its standard through practical assessment.

variants.name: Renewable credential
variants.description: The credential expires after a set period and must be renewed by fresh assessment or evidence of practice.

mechanics: Goal-setting; assessment; signalling; mastery learning
cautions: People study to pass the test and stop there. Assess real tasks, and keep practice on the job going after the certificate.
theory: Goal-setting; assessment; signalling; mastery learning
howTo: Find out whether a recognised credential already exists and whether it matches the job. Use it if it does.
If you build your own, define the standard in terms of what people must do, and who will recognise it.
Design the assessment first, and include a practical task as well as a knowledge test.
Build the learning path back from the assessment, with practice on tasks like the real ones.
Train the assessors and check that they mark the same work the same way.
Set an expiry date or a renewal requirement if the field changes fast.
time: Weeks to months, depending on the level
group: Individuals or cohorts, any number
